Title: Gemini Decisions API: Fast, calibrated multimodal decisions

URL Source: https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/developers-tools/gemini-decisions-api/

Published Time: 2026-11-11T18:00:00+00:00

Markdown Content:

5 min read

Introducing the Gemini Decisions API, powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model. Evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no, choice, and rubric-scoring questions in a fast, single pass across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs.

* * *

Min Choi

Product Manager, Google DeepMind

Felix Yu

Principal Scientist, Google DeepMind

* * *

Listen to article

[[duration]] minutes

This content is generated by Google AI. Generative AI is experimental

Today, we’re introducing the Gemini Decisions API, a new endpoint for fast, closed-set decisions powered by our new Gemini Decision 1 model (gemini-decision-1), available through the [Gemini API](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/decisions-api) in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/gemini-decisions-api-playground?fullscreenApplet=true).

The Decisions API gives you purpose-built primitives for bounded choices like tool selection, policy checks, model routing, and context grading. You can pass one multimodal input across text, images, audio, video, and PDFs (up to 256K tokens) along with up to 1,000 independent questions. Rather than generating answer text token by token, Gemini Decision 1 scores your candidate options in a single forward pass, returning probabilities and confidence scores in 150-250 ms end-to-end latency at $0.10 per 1M input tokens with zero output tokens billed.

## Strong performance and calibration

On benchmarks spanning agent routing, reasoning, ranking, and multimodal understanding, Gemini Decision 1 leads across the suite, with the lowest calibration error.

Gemini Decision 1 scores options without token-by-token decoding, keeping median latency 50-100 ms of model compute (150-250 ms end-to-end), across multimodal inputs and contexts up to 16K tokens, remaining nearly flat from 1 to 100 questions per request. With zero output tokens billed, Gemini Decision 1 with the Decisions API is nearly 5x cheaper across the shared benchmark suite than Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with the Interactions API.

## Native multimodal evaluation across three decision types in one pass

Built on Gemini’s native multimodal architecture, Gemini Decision 1 can process text, images, audio, video, and PDFs directly in a single forward pass. You can combine modalities in one shared input, such as pairing a call recording with account metadata or a scanned PDF claim with damage photos, and tune resolution on image and video inputs to control visual detail and token cost.

You can evaluate multiple questions against that shared input in a single request, mixing yes/no checks, multiple choice, and rubric scores. Every answer includes a confidence score (from 0 to 1) so your code can route ambiguous cases to a fallback or human reviewer:

*   **noul (Yes/No):** Estimates the probability that a yes/no condition holds, with optional true and false description criteria.
*   **choice (Multiple Choice):** Selects from 2 to 255 choices, returning the winner and normalized probabilities for every candidate.
*   **score (Ordered Rubric):** Grades inputs across an ordered rubric (starting at 0), returning a continuous weighted score and per-level probabilities.

The `input` field uses the same `Content` block format as the [Interactions API](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/interactions-overview). Here is how to check a photo of a breakroom counter, together with a text note, against all three question types in one request:

## How teams are building with the Decisions API

Teams across Google are already using the Decisions API as a low-latency control plane, shipping features simply by defining options rather than training custom classifiers or waiting on generative calls:

*   **Dynamic model routing in Gemini Notebook:** Gemini Notebook uses the Decisions API as a real-time router to instantly direct incoming queries to the optimal model tier and thinking level for each request. The Decisions API classifies intent in milliseconds to serve everyday queries with up to 40% lower latency while reserving deep reasoning models for complex tasks.
*   **Rapid design iteration in Stitch:** The new [rapid canvas experiment in Stitch](https://stitch.withgoogle.com/rapid) uses the Decisions API to generate playable wireframes of a product flow in seconds and to apply edits made by voice or tap almost instantly. When the flow feels right, one click hands the screens off to the full Stitch experience for deeper design polish.
*   **Emoji selection in CC:** CC from Google Labs uses the Decisions API to pick the right emoji reaction from a palette of more than 200 options in a fraction of a second, so reactions appear instantly without adding latency.
*   **Safety layer for MCP tools in Search**: Google Search uses the Decision API to detect adversarial behavior and content against adversarial evals with high efficacy within the latency envelope.

Stitch Rapid uses the Decisions API to design an entire product flow in seconds (1x speed).

## Start building today

Gemini Decision 1 is priced at $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $0 for output tokens, with an API no-cost tier you can use in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/gemini-decisions-api-playground?fullscreenApplet=true) for prototyping. Your shared `input` is billed once per request no matter how many questions you evaluate (each question adds only its own instruction and criteria tokens). There are no output-token charges, variable thinking-token bills, or separate audio transcription and OCR costs.

You can start building today by grabbing an API key in [Google AI Studio](https://aistudio.google.com/api-keys), trying our [Doorstep Parcels](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/doorstep-parcels-qa?fullscreenApplet=true), [Speed Sketch](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/speed-sketch?fullscreenApplet=true), and [Find the Zoo Keeper](https://aistudio.google.com/apps/bundled/find-the-zoo-keeper?fullscreenApplet=true) demo apps, and following the Python, JavaScript, and REST guides in the [Decisions API documentation](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/decisions-api).

Ecosystem integrations are rolling out across [OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/google/gemini-decision-1), [LangChain](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/integrations/providers/google), [Vercel](https://ai-sdk.dev/providers/ai-sdk-providers/google), [LiteLLM](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/providers/gemini), [Pydantic AI](https://pydantic.dev/docs/ai/models/google/), [Pipecat](https://docs.pipecat.ai/api-reference/server/classifiers/google), [LiveKit](https://docs.livekit.io/agents/integrations/google/), and [OpenCode](https://opencode.ai/) alongside the `google-genai` SDKs, with support [coming soon](https://forms.gle/NFt1W6pL1gCY9FGM8) to Gemini in Google Cloud.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

[Gilbert + Tobin⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.gtlaw.com.au/) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information.

Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval.

We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs.

Video interview with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.

## Sam, what is Gilbert + Tobin trying to achieve with AI?

We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market.

The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry.

> _“It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.”_

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You describe Gilbert + Tobin’s journey in three phases: experimentation, personal productivity, and organisational productivity. How did the firm get started?

When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment.

The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients.

Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work.

## You’ve noticed that adoption is unusually high for your firm, with 87% active usage among enabled ChatGPT users, more than twice the rate Gilbert + Tobin typically sees for other tools. How did leadership shape that culture?

Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it.

We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm.

Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team.

> _“Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.”_

—Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer, Gilbert + Tobin

## You have made ChatGPT central to your own work. What have you learned from what you’ve built?

To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins)using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports.

My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place.

I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes.

With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days.

## What advice would you give other CEOs beginning this journey?

Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters.

Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result.

The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value.

**Find out more about Gilbert + Tobin’s work with OpenAI through the case study**[**here**](https://openai.com/index/gilbert-tobin/)**.**

## 20,000 veterans are using ChatGPT to build what comes next

In the past year, more than 20,000 transitioning servicemembers and veterans have claimed a year of [ChatGPT Plus at no cost](https://openai.com/index/chatgpt-for-veterans/) after being offered free access by OpenAI. That milestone gives us a chance to look at how veterans are using AI to prepare for civilian careers and to figure out what comes next for themselves and their families.

The effort started with veterans who work here at OpenAI, people who use these tools every day and know firsthand how challenging the transition can be. Beyond the free access, OpenAI Academy and our community partners have hosted more than a dozen trainings for nearly 1,000 members of the military community, [with seven more⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/home/events) scheduled before the year ends.

## Preparing for civilian careers

Leaving the military often means stepping into an unfamiliar job market and working out how years of service translate into a civilian role. Many veterans are turning to ChatGPT to organize their job search, rehearse for interviews, and explore paths they hadn’t considered.

## Learning to use ChatGPT, together

Not everyone arrives confident about using AI tools, which is why OpenAI Academy gives veterans, transitioning servicemembers, and military spouses a place to learn alongside people who understand what they’re going through.

OpenAI recently wrapped our first six-event Academy series with [Veterans Forge⁠(opens in a new window)](https://veteransforge.org/), focused on helping veterans and military families use ChatGPT to work toward their goals. That pilot, together with workshops alongside AI Collective Hampton Roads and NPower, is shaping what we offer veterans next.

At one [workshop in Reston, Virginia⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/en/public/events/openai-academy-for-veterans-w8zz8dfrts), nearly [100 veterans and active-duty servicemembers⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) explored ways to put AI to work. Participant [Ryan Kaono-Wedemeyer⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/in/ryan-kaono-wedemeyer) learned to start by writing out a detailed account of his military experience, then asking AI to help shape it into a civilian résumé.

Instructor [Erin Marie⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/erinrosemarie_veterans-ai-aicommunity-activity-7440044135958384640-j7S-) helped participants build custom GPTs to support their transitions, and watched people who walked in skeptical begin finding ways the tools could genuinely help them.

In Louisville, Kentucky, [more than 80 Legionnaires⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/veterans-forge_theamericanlegion-veteransforge-veterans-activity-7499820737151541248-PqzY) attended three AI training sessions at the American Legion’s national convention. For those who can’t make it to an event, our [online veterans collection⁠(opens in a new window)](https://academy.openai.com/public/collections/veterans) and [100 chats for veterans⁠(opens in a new window)](https://chatgpt.com/use-cases/veterans?openaicom-did=1d367852-8bd6-4a81-b3c2-c9be979c7377&openaicom_referred=true) offer examples to try on your own.

## What’s next

We’re continuing this work with partners across the country through the rest of the year:

Our goal is to help veterans and military families carry the skills they built in service into whatever work they choose next. We’re grateful to [ID.me⁠(opens in a new window)](http://id.me/) for helping servicemembers and veterans access the free-year offer, and to our community partners for making these events possible.

This Veterans Day, OpenAI thanks veterans for their service and for contributing to their communities.

# Try Tabletop: Customizable, collaborative spaces for groups to plan, play and do more together.

Roman Nurik

Design & Engineering Lead, Google Labs

Nov 11, 2026

* * *

Whether you’re planning a family trip, running a rec league or hosting a potluck, coordinating as a group is easier when everyone can pitch in, build and decide together in one place.

Today, we’re introducing [Tabletop](https://tabletop.google/), a new Google Labs experiment built for real-time collaboration.

Just add in your links, files, and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters, and tournament brackets. Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time, like in a Google Doc.

Tabletop is rolling out in the U.S. (18+) via waitlist. Pull up a chair and sign up at [labs.google/tabletop](http://labs.google/tabletop).

Today we’re sharing the [first online retrospective of artist Dr. Esther Mahlangu](https://artsandculture.google.com/project/esther-mahlangu) on Google Arts & Culture, honoring her pioneering spirit on her 91st birthday. More than 45 stories and a rich archive covering her [art](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/_QVhsTxpEWbtnQ), [life](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/TQWRPyjN0Luu_g), and [legacy](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/AQUxh9rtUMe9mQ) are now accessible to a global audience.

For many years, I have worked closely with Esther and her family. It’s a relationship built on years of research and a deep admiration for her as both an artist and a person. It was out of this long-standing connection that the vision for “‘[Then I Knew I Was Good at Painting’: Esther Mahlangu, a Retrospective](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/cAVhFwrQ8k2kag),” was born.

My goal has always been to present a comprehensive exploration of her life and work, contributing to my long-standing research on South African women artists who have made an impact on the arts since the early 20th century.

Through my research, I gathered a rich collection of her work, including [large-scale murals](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/9wWRh4woZhmiOg), [intimate pieces](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/kgVhZwuHYWhn1g), and [rare archival materials](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/9AUB-bLz0QU8DQ). But the archives didn’t include anything from her life before 1980, so crucial pieces of her history were missing. This void challenged us to find new ways to tell her full story.

A collaboration session with Esther Mahlangu, Nontobeko Ntombela, and the Google team.

In collaboration with Google Arts & Culture, we used [AI to visually recreate Esther’s undocumented memories](https://youtu.be/FWhQt-NfIKw). The process brought us closer to her work and prompted further recollections from Esther herself.

This project brought our curatorial and archival work together with the technical expertise of Google DeepMind and Google Arts & Culture Lab, alongside research and design studio Domestic Data Streamers’ synthetic memories initiative. Through a series of [workshops and interviews](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/OwUBQR258WOrrw), we were able to [document a missing period](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/iQUxnW9XyhhFQg) of Mam' Esther's history, from when she started painting at age 10 until her first documented works in 1980. These stories — such as [the moment she discovered her talent for painting as a 10-year-old](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/JwXRghigf-9lOw) using feathers instead of a brush — became the source material for our work. Following the methodology from the [synthetic memories initiative](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/synthetic-memories/ewVh6MMjnKk7Yg) and using archival material, the team generated still images based on Esther’s memories. They then used [Veo](https://deepmind.google/models/veo/) to turn the images into videos that brought Esther's early days to life.

The stories also contribute to the online archive of Esther’s life on Google Arts & Culture. More than [45 exhibitions](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/exhibit?project=esther-mahlangu), curated in collaboration with Art of Contemporary Africa, Iziko Museums of South Africa, the British Museum, the Jean Pigozzi Collection, the National Museum of Women in the Arts, and Serpentine, tell the story of [how she came to be known](https://artsandculture.google.com/story/CwXRnb-h-CMBpA) in the world, through her [artwork](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/asset?project=esther-mahlangu-explore-artworks), archives, [Street View](https://artsandculture.google.com/search/streetview?project=esther-mahlangu), and more.

> Thank you to Google Arts &Culture for sharing my story, artwork, and the culture of the Ndebele nation with the world. It has always been my wish to ensure that the art and culture of my Nation lives on for those who follow.

By Dr. Esther Mahlangu

> We're honored to help celebrate Dr. Esther Mahlangu’s legacy by making her work globally accessible online, offering younger generations everywhere the chance to explore Ndebele heritage and be inspired by her pioneering vision.

By Amit Sood VP of Google Arts & Culture

This project demonstrates a new way to approach the preservation of cultural heritage, with technology that’s guided at every step by a respect for personal memory and historical accuracy.

It is my hope that this retrospective cements Esther’s place as a pivotal voice in global contemporary art, invites audiences to reimagine the possibilities of her archive, and ensures her story and her artistic vision can inspire generations to come.

Title: How AI Helps Recyclers Turn Mixed Waste Into Reusable Material

URL Source: https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/ai-recycling-startups/

Published Time: 2026-11-11T03:00:20+00:00

Markdown Content:
Vision AI and robotics pick what’s worth recovering out of conveyor belts of used clothing, bottles and mixed recyclables, diverting thousands of tons of materials from landfills.

As world leaders gather for COP31 in Türkiye, the event’s [emphasis on zero waste](https://cop.sifiratikvakfi.org/en/news/president-erdogans-cop31-call-zero-waste-movement-is-the-strongest-bridge/) puts a practical challenge in focus: how to keep products and materials in use for longer. Globally, [less than 7%](https://circularity-gap.world/updates-collection/global-circularity-rate-fell-to-6-9---despite-growing-recycling) of the materials entering the economy come from recycled or reused sources. Municipal solid waste generation accounts for over [2 billion tons](https://www.unep.org/en/publications/report/global-waste-management-outlook-2024) of trash per year — a figure that could [nearly double by 2050](https://www.weforum.org/stories/nature-and-biodiversity/circular-economy-waste-management-unep).

AI and robotics are helping change this trajectory, as innovators around the globe improve sorting to recover resources that would otherwise end up in landfills.

“A more circular economy relies on making better use of what we already have,” said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at NVIDIA. “AI can help us understand what’s in a waste stream, identify what can be recovered and automate the work of sorting it. We’re giving innovators the computing tools to make those processes more effective and bring them to more places.”

See how four members of the [NVIDIA Inception](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) program for startups are applying AI to keep valuable materials in circulation.

## **AIRECO Gives Plastic Waste New Life**

Recycled plastic is only used if its cost and quality can compete with new material. Too often it can’t: Incoming waste is of inconsistent quality, sorting depends on hard-to-find manual labor and mixed scrap ends up downcycled into low-grade products.

The founders of AIRECO, a Taiwan-based startup, believe that AI sorting can cut down the cost and improve the quality of recycling to make these materials more commercially useful. The company uses vision AI to sort plastics more finely, enabling materials to be plucked out of mixed scrap piles for closed-loop recycling, where used items are reprocessed into new versions of the same product.

“The finer you sort, the more you can recycle,” said Chun-Feng Liu, founder and CEO of AIRECO. “With finely sorted material, it’s more likely that an item can stay in the loop — a plastic bottle recycled back into a bottle again and again, rather than ending up in other products that are hard to recycle further.”

The company uses [NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules to run inference across its pilot line at a recycling plant in Tainan, including to drive robotic arms that pick targets off a conveyor belt. Recognition accuracy on the test line tops 95%.

In a full production line planned for next year, the team aims to nearly triple annual waste processing capacity from 18,000 to 48,000 tons while cutting operating costs by 85%.

## **EverestLabs AI Puts Robotics on the Recycling Line**

At material recovery facilities, the plants that separate household recyclables, sorting must be done in real time at fast-moving conveyor belts — requiring rapid analysis to identify and sort items.

EverestLabs AI, a U.S. startup, deploys computer vision-guided robots on those sorting lines. About 150 robots are currently deployed in facilities across North America and Australia.

“Other robots have infinite time to finish their tasks,” said R. Paul Singh, CEO of EverestLabs AI. “We don’t have that luxury because our conveyor belts are going to come in at a certain speed, and we have to act at a fast clip before the material moves. It’s a real-time game.”

EverestLabs runs AI inference on NVIDIA RTX GPUs at the edge and trains its models on [NVIDIA data center GPUs](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/technologies/rubin/), optimized using NVIDIA CUDA. The company estimates its deployed systems have so far identified about 40 billion objects, recycled roughly 25,000 tons of material and avoided about 30,000 metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.

Their team is constantly working to improve its models to correctly classify and pick every kind of object while capturing metadata about the material type, brand and packaging of each. They’re also shipping agentic AI tools to provide actionable data to recycling facility staff, from floor managers to executives responsible for multiple facilities — and are looking to extend that capability to adjacent industries.

## **Greyparrot Gives Recyclers a Clear View of the Waste Stream**

Recycling plants can process tens of thousands of tons of waste a day, yet operators have long judged what’s on the belt by manually sampling less than 1% of it.

U.K. startup Greyparrot built its Analyzer platform to change that. Mounted above conveyor belts, it uses computer vision to identify each passing object by material and brand, even in dusty environments or poor lighting on belts moving up to 4 meters a second.

“Waste changes all the time. It shifts by hour, by season, by supplier,” said Ambarish Mitra, cofounder of Greyparrot. “Before, operators guessed based on a tiny sample, and now they can see exactly what’s on the belt.”

Greyparrot uses NVIDIA GPUs to train AI models on billions of objects, while NVIDIA Jetson modules run rapid detection at the edge. More than 300 Analyzer systems, operating in over 20 countries, have made over a trillion bounding box detections to date — reducing the time needed to check 15 tons of waste from 375 hours to just six.

Facilities using the real-time data from Analyzer report efficiency gains of 10% to 30%. At global packaging company Amcor, the solution helped increase the yield of [food-grade plastics by 12%](https://www.greyparrot.ai/resources/case-studies/amcor-case-study-a-12-lift-in-food-grade-polypropylene-yield). Brands including Coca-Cola, Colgate-Palmolive and Kenvue also use Greyparrot technology to measure how their packaging is recycled in real sorting plants.

## **reverse.fashion Gives Discarded Garments a Second Look**

Europe generates [nearly 7 million tons](https://www.eea.europa.eu/en/analysis/publications/management-of-used-and-waste-textiles-in-europes-circular-economy) of used textiles a year. About a quarter of these textiles are collected separately and sorted by hand into hundreds of categories, destined for uses ranging from vintage resale to downcycling as furniture filling or cleaning cloths. The work is slow, costly and hard to staff, which keeps the value of reusable garments buried.

reverse.fashion, a Berlin-based startup, is helping automate the job with high-resolution computer vision. Its system identifies product type, defects, color, size, brand, fabric construction, season and style and assigns each garment to its most valuable category.

“Compared to classical waste sorting, our AI models have to run at very high resolution because humans are picky with textiles,” said Karsten Pufahl, cofounder and chief technology officer of reverse.fashion. “The computer vision pipeline needs to spot small defects to determine the quality and potential value of each garment.”

As it moves across a conveyor belt at 3 meters a second, each textile analyzed by Reverse Fashion passes through over a dozen vision AI models optimized with [NVIDIA TensorRT](https://developer.nvidia.com/tensorrt) software and running on [NVIDIA Jetson](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/autonomous-machines/embedded-systems/) modules at the edge. The models are trained on NVIDIA GPUs in workstations and the cloud.

The system sorts in an hour what would’ve previously taken a week to sort, Pufahl estimates, and is currently rolling out to facilities in Europe.

articles.content:
Nvidia co-founder CEO Jensen Huang has never been as flashy or controversy-prone as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. Now, the 63-year-old industry kingpin has admitted that he
cheated on his wife
of 40 years in an affair that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and potentially impact national security.
United States officials believe that Huang’s likely romantic interest, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is
a Chinese spy
who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)
Megaspeed, a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company, had reportedly
purchased
$4.8 billion in Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, the Times has reported.
The story took a sudden new turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also
had an extramarital relationship
with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of health care, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.
Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board is preparing to
oust Huang
, and Nvidia’s shares fell in after-hours trading.
The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
After reports of a second extramarital affair, Nvidia’s board reportedly plans to meet to discuss Huang’s future at the company, per the Wall Street Journal. Stock fell
about 8%
in after hours trading on Wednesday and is down 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he
has said
. The company has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan.
November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says
The New York Times
reported
that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.
According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.
November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair
Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressman to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China committee Chairman Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be
subpoenaed
.
November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements
The Nvidia CEO pulled out of
upcoming speaking engagements
at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.
November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy
Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips,
The Information reported
. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.
Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International,
Bloomberg reported
. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.
In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs,
the Financial Times reported.
November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”
On Sunday night, President Trump
weighed in
on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.
When asked if Huang
should remain chief of Nvidia
, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”
November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation
Jensen Huang wrote in a
letter
to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”
“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.
Nvidia shares slid
over 5%
the following day.
November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing
Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.
“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen
wrote
. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”
October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy
U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when
the New York Times
broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.
An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.
“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”
Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy
U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later
reported
by the New York Times.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio
supervised
the drafting of the memo.
Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action
Around the same time, per the New York Times’
report
, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.
The Nvidia CEO, an
ally of Trump
, has
repeatedly advocated
for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.
October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations
Megaspeed was
confirmed
to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was
suspected
of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.
Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.
Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.
These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”
“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson
said
at the time.

articles.content:
CoreWeave is rewriting how it pays for the AI boom, according to the
company’s third-quarter earnings
, reported on Tuesday. CoreWeave, a neocloud that rents out the computing power behind AI, said it’s increasingly asking customers to pay up front, borrowing against specific contracts, and even pursuing short-term deals that could lead to higher prices.
The new strategies could help CoreWeave finance its growth more efficiently while squeezing more cash from existing infrastructure. But these bets only hold if today’s demand and pricing power continue.
CoreWeave reported $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% from the year prior, but it also posted a $709 million net loss and $846 million in quarterly interest expense.
“We will not use the unsecured debt market to fund our business at current yields, nor do we need to,” CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said during Tuesday’s earnings call.
Instead, CoreWeave’s plan is to rely on loans backed by specific customer contracts, drawing on funds as needed to finance most of the infrastructure it still has to build to deliver on its significant backlog of $132.5 billion.
CoreWeave also said it expects about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months, including more than $3 billion tied to signing new customer contracts for capacity it has already built, which requires no additional spending on hardware.
Rivals Nebius and IREN have also relied on hefty Microsoft prepayments to pay for computing capacity, signaling that the industry is moving toward asking Big Tech to pay up for their buildouts.
Upfront payments could alleviate CoreWeave’s immediate borrowing needs, but they also commit the company to providing services at a price that might be less attractive down the road if compute demand continues to surge.
CoreWeave is also looking to capitalize on that growing demand by signing more shorter-term contracts that can command much higher prices.
The company raised prices across its offerings by about 25% in July and by another 10% later in the quarter. Prices are still climbing this quarter, in a way that “more than offset[s] cost increases,” said Intrator.
“We are also allocating more capacity to short-term opportunities, where the pricing justifies it, selling capacity at more than $40 million per megawatt annually, while pricing for new infrastructure on four- and five-year contracts is moving to $20 million to $25 million per megawatt,” the chief executive said.
CoreWeave’s financing strategy now revolves around those opportunities. In August, the company closed a $2.6 billion loan, its first designed specifically for shorter-term customer contracts. Known as DDTL 5.5, it lets CoreWeave borrow in installments as it needs the money.
While short-term deals let CoreWeave charge higher prices and change them more frequently, it’s a trade-off. Lenders give more weight to longer-term contracts, even if they’re priced lower, because they value predictable cash flow and consistency to repay the loan above all.
Even though Wall Street reacted positively to CoreWeave’s earnings, bond investors are much less sanguine. Last month, yields on some of the
company’s bonds hit above 15%,
highlighting that investors are concerned about the debt needed to fund data center buildouts before those investments see a return.
In short, CoreWeave is finding new ways to expand without relying on unsecured debt. The strategy it has chosen could boost profits, but it also carries greater risk around contract renewals and pricing — and it just goes to show how dependent the AI infrastructure boom is on sustained, and as yet unproven, demand.
TechCrunch has reached out to CoreWeave for more information about its loan facility.

Fractile
, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised
a $720 million Series C
backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government
stated
.
Alongside the likes of
Axelera
,
Etched
, and
OLIX
, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production.
However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips.
As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both
by the Financial Times
and
a Reuters source
.
Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a
pivot
, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity.
This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date.
In a
LinkedIn post
, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.”

articles.content:
The AI industry is still reeling from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s honeypot scandal, but some in the industry see it as an issue that’s much larger than one man.
The Chinese government has been active in economic espionage for decades, and with semiconductors at the center of the AI boom, there’s intense pressure to infiltrate any company involved. At the same time, many of the executives getting rich off that boom have made themselves easy targets.
As CEO of investment intel firm Heron Intelligence, Nate Singer has a unique view into the problem. His firm works on corporate due diligence: Essentially, making sure companies know the relevant dirt before making a major acquisition or executive hire. And while the Nvidia case is particularly severe, Singer says there are lots of similar cases in the semiconductor industry that have stayed under the radar.
“We’ve got former employees talking about behavior at senior executive levels,” Singer told TechCrunch, saying executives are “really crossing lines that should not be crossed.”
In
a widely circulated LinkedIn post
, Singer detailed one case in which a CEO’s wife made an unexpected board room appearance, “screaming about her husband and another company exec flying around in the corporate jet with a couple young ladies (who also turned out to be state-sponsored actors).”
It’s an alarming story, but an unfortunately common one. Singer says he’s seen at least three reports of similar cases, and suspects many more have gone unreported.
“There’s a lot more than this one woman,” Singer said. “They are embedded in these companies.”
Semiconductor companies are already big targets for international trade secret theft. There have been
dozens of prosecutions
for similar cases in recent years, including
a case involving the fabrication powerhouse TSMC
in 2007.
In 2017, four executives at
an unnamed “Bay Area semiconductor equipment manufacturer”
were charged with stealing trade secrets for use at a competing company in China. According to the indictment, the technology in question “related to the high-volume manufacturing of semiconductor wafers to be used in lighting and electronic devices, such as flat screen televisions and smart phones.“
Any sexual elements in such cases rarely become public, in part because of the severe consequences for executives and their companies. But according to Singer, the ongoing threat has become a kind of open secret in the industry.
“There are a lot of senior people in the industry that know this is happening, and are effectively condoning it,” he told TechCrunch.

articles.content:
OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models,
Bloomberg reported
, citing anonymous sources.
If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company
reportedly
recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year.
OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said.
OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses.
But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently
reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion
. OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has
over a billion users
, but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans.
Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth.
OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks.
OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is
seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon
, said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October.
(Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.)
None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open source AI labs, especially those from China.

articles.content:
Databricks on Wednesday unveiled an updated version of its AI agent Genie, which can now perform multistep jobs that take extended work to finish. It does this through an ontology that Databricks built to give Genie the context it needs from the information that customers store on the Databricks platform.
Corporate leaders can now assign the agent a wide range of tasks, and it will complete them unsupervised, the company says. To prove the point, Databricks CEO Ali Ghodsi showed me how he uses it internally. Instead of a product demo, he fired up his actual agent and walked me through his most recent chats and charts.
He showed me how it analyzed the parts of an employee satisfaction survey where the company didn’t score well, and how it helped him rate (and discard) fixes for those low scores that some executives suggested. He showed me how it summarized a big sales pitch to a prospect that went poorly — including the features the prospect said it needed before buying.
It also prepped him for a podcast interview by reviewing his previous appearances and developing likely questions. While we talked, he even had it tell him what he should say to me. (And its advice on that wasn’t bad.)
The fascinating part was that Ghodsi was using Genie to find the stuff that he’s now unlikely to hear as the big boss. It was a source of unvarnished truth about what wasn’t going well that he needed to address.
“Have you heard of Dunbar’s number? The magic number is 150,” he said when I pointed this out. Named for British anthropologist Robin Dunbar, it’s theoretically the maximum number of people with whom humans can maintain stable relationships. In a small startup, a CEO knows everyone, has direct relationships with them, and they feel safe to tell him negative info straight up.
With 12,000 employees, Ghodsi is the first to admit he can’t know everyone. At that size, a salesperson isn’t likely to confess a disastrous sales call to the CEO. An HR manager isn’t likely to confess that their idea for increasing employee satisfaction will probably fail.
“Anyone who has more than 150 employees, which is a lot of companies, a lot of people can get value out of this,” he said of AI agents generally and his product, Genie, specifically.
Ghodsi’s own use of Genie (often called dogfooding, from the phrase “eating your own dogfood”) is one reason why Databricks is now pitching it as an always-on agent for business leaders. He says he also uses it in his personal life, rather than a security-questionable alternative like OpenClaw or Instinct or Muse.
He believes Genie can do for the business side what AI, agents, and harnesses (the software that wraps around an AI model and lets it use tools) are doing for programmers. As for the risk that agents will ratchet up corporate AI costs, Ghodsi has an answer for that, too. He said costs can be controlled through Databricks’ Unity Gateway product. It allows companies to set usage limits and to swap in less expensive open-weight models.

articles.content:
AI agents are all the rage, but they’re not quite as capable as their purveyors would have you believe.
Efforts to benchmark agents doing complex tasks show that they aren’t typically reliable enough to function without close supervision. LiveBench 2.0
shows
Claude Fable 5.2 and ChatGPT-6 Astra succeeding on 82.9 and 75.6 out of 100 tasks, respectively, and
an effort
by the AI infrastructure company EON to test agents in a simulated corporate environment found the most successful model tested, Claude Opus 4.8, performed tasks at 76.8% accuracy.
Now, a startup known as Plurai wants to boost those numbers with the same techniques that put self-driving cars on the street: Simulations using synthetic data based on a company’s own digital systems, meant to prepare models to tackle difficult edge cases.
Co-founders Ilan Kadar and Elad Levi previously worked for Nexar, which develops autonomous driving technology. Kadar worked with Waymo to simulate and evaluate its end-to-end deep learning driving software.
“The moment that we saw the wave of AI agents, we saw the same pattern: That it is very easy to build a demo, but [hard] to get something that will be reliable and cost effective,” Kadar told TechCrunch. “Since we saw the same pattern, the same pitch was that we want to build this simulation layer.”
On Wednesday, the startup said it had raised $13 million in seed funding to make that happen. The round was led by Team8, with participation from U&I, Velocity, and Mercer.
Like the end-to-end models trained to drive cars, AI agents are probabilistic systems operating in unpredictable environments. When pressed by customers, agents tasked with booking travel can ignore spending policies. Or, when tasked with querying one database, agents can reliably provide an answer, but combining information from multiple datasets tends to gum up the works. A long conversation with a customer service bot can overwhelm an agent with too much context and lead to wrong turns.
To fix that, Plurai creates a digital twin of the company’s electronic systems, including the knowledge base and tools that an agent will have access to in production. It then maps all the possible flows of the agents and uses that graph to prepare the model with evaluations and fixes for possible edge cases. The platform works alongside existing agentic tools like Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, and Cursor.
However, Kadar says the company’s real promise is using the data it gathers to post-train small, open-weight models tailored to individual customer needs. Tests performed in cooperation with Nvidia and Nebius
showed
the company’s models outperforming midtier frontier models at lower costs.
“We can take a large language model, we can take the task, decompose it into a smaller task using the simulation, train [an open-weight] model, and using the simulation, verify that the quality is higher or comparable to the frontier model, and an order or two orders of magnitude cost reduction,” he said.
Reah Miyara, a Google DeepMind researcher who backed Plurai as an angel investor, said the company’s edge comes from understanding failure modes in production, and generating synthetic data to tune models. As businesses try to optimize their AI expense, Plurai’s approach could prove a real advantage, since IT leaders are seeing that “frontier-capable models are out of distribution with my specific data, and the cost of these things isn’t sustainable in the long term,” Miyara said.
Plurai hopes analogies between AI agents in physical and digital environments can prove predictive: While powerful general AI models are imbuing robots with fascinating capabilities, they aren’t yet reliable enough to be deployed widely. Meanwhile, robots powered by AI models built for specific tasks are in the field right now, working for customers and gathering valuable real-world data.
“My view is that no matter how smart OpenAI and Anthropic model will be — and they will be much smarter — they will not know your business and your policy,” Kadar said.

articles.content:
Nvidia’s stock sank 5.47% on Tuesday, following a 4% drop on Monday, a loss of about 9.5% in two days, even though there wasn’t much news out of the company. CEO Jensen Huang has reportedly been trying to conduct
business as usual
after admitting to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The biggest development: the board hired the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an internal investigation.
What comes next is mostly a guessing game, even for the people who study how boards are supposed to handle crises. Two corporate governance professors, Ann Lipton of the University of Colorado and Todd Henderson of the University of Chicago, say there is no real precedent for a CEO caught up in a suspected honeypot. And while they have views on what the investigation should ask, like everyone else, they’re watching to see how it plays out.
“There have actually been affair cases and sexual harassment cases,” Lipton said, but she was quick to add that she doesn’t know of previous cases that also involve potential national security compromises. Henderson, whose research interests include corporations, securities regulation, and law and economics, said much depends on facts few people have yet, including, most importantly, what, if anything, Alice Huang got out of Jensen Huang. (Secrets about Nvidia’s fabs or chip designs would matter to the Justice Department. Ordinary corporate information probably would not.)
Lipton described the investigation led by Nvidia’s independent board members, with their own outside counsel, as perhaps the most “standard” aspect of the whole affair so far. She also observed that an investigation will be “exactly as thorough” as the directors running it want it to be, which is also standard. Henderson made a related point about incentives, saying that Washington law firms that conduct internal investigations “know who pays their bills.” He didn’t suggest that’s happening here.
Lipton said she sees three lines of inquiry, including whether the law was broken, whether Huang violated Nvidia’s internal policies, and whether the board was misled, including how forthcoming he was and when he was on notice. It’s notable, as Wired
reported Monday
, that Huang hired a PR crisis firm known for handling sex scandals a full year ago. Of course, the driver could have been about the affair alone. It’s unclear when Huang learned Alice Huang was a suspected spy. The board said in a Sunday
statement
about the matter that Nvidia “has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”
Henderson similarly stressed the importance of what Huang knew and when. He described two scenarios. In one, Huang hires a PR firm because an extramarital affair is embarrassing, without knowing who the woman is. In the other, he knows she is a suspected Chinese spy. “I think that’s very different,” he said. “If I were a board member and the CEO of a company with very sensitive technology was in that situation, I would be furious if they didn’t tell me.” Not telling the board that you have cancer “or that you’ve been sleeping with a Chinese spy,” said Henderson, “seems to me to be a fireable offense.”
Either way, Lipton expects shareholder suits, and she said two kinds are possible. Securities fraud, which she said is “only about lying,” is the most obvious, and as we reported yesterday, Nvidia is
already facing a proposed class action lawsuit
that alleges Nvidia and Huang misled investors by concealing Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang while describing dealings with her former employer as routine. “You can have as many affairs with Chinese spies as you like,” Lipton said. “You just can’t lie about it under the federal securities laws.”
A mismanagement claim under Delaware law, where Nvidia is incorporated, is much harder. Employees do “stupid or reckless or damaging things all the time,” she said, and courts don’t let shareholders sue each time. Shareholders bringing such a claim on the company’s behalf, known as a derivative suit, must first show the board is incapable of handling the problem, usually by proving directors are implicated or so beholden to the CEO that they can’t act independently.
Nvidia’s 10-member board has a track record of
loyalty and deference
to Huang, as outlined by a New York Times piece Tuesday morning. Still, the investigation those “independent” directors have announced with outside counsel makes that very hard. Lipton cited, for example, a shareholder suit over alleged mismanagement at McDonald’s several years ago, after its chief people officer was accused of harassment and its CEO had a relationship with a subordinate. Ultimately, the court found no reason the board couldn’t deal with the misconduct on its own.
Even if none of this ends up threatening Huang’s job, the episode raises other governance questions that don’t look great in retrospect. Nvidia is run with a famously flat structure, with more than 60 direct reports to Huang, and the company doesn’t appear to have a succession plan, which Lipton called “a danger for any company.”
Huang’s children also work at Nvidia. His son Spencer is a director of product management, his daughter Madison is a senior director of product marketing, and his son-in-law, Nico Caprez, works in business development. Some employees believe Huang is grooming successors, and
when asked last month by Bloomberg
whether Madison is in line for the job, Huang didn’t shoot down the idea, saying instead that it’s not something he’d wish on her.
Lipton called hiring the kids poor corporate hygiene, even though founders have long done it. (Kimbal Musk is on Tesla’s board because he’s Elon Musk’s brother, she noted.) Directors are supposed to act only for stockholders, but founders get more rope as long as the company is thriving.
Henderson similarly calls himself a strong “anti-nepotism person,” sharing that when his father worked at Westinghouse’s nuclear research lab, there was an absolute ban on hiring employees’ children. “Like, fine for them to be working there,” he said of Huang’s children working at Nvidia. But “the idea that one of his kids would succeed him” at a publicly traded company the size of Nvidia “seems crazy,” he added.
What Nvidia may have gotten more right, from a governance standpoint, is what it doesn’t have, which is dual-class shares. Huang reportedly owns about 3.6%, so he doesn’t control the vote. That makes him “easier to dislodge,” Lipton said, even though he is deeply integrated into the company in other ways.
Neither professor is rooting for or against Huang, each made clear. The simple truth is that with voting control on top of Huang’s holdings, the board would have even less flexibility. Without it, the board has a few more options.

Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments.
AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was
released last year
. While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell.
The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a
blog post
published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
Related
Google’s Atlas of the human genome could pave the way for new treatments
Anthropic wants to develop its own drugs
AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases —
huge data repositories that map and catalog
individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model.
Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.
For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told
The Verge
.
Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told
The Verge
that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital.
Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “
virtual cells
,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems.
Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide
Atlas
covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September.
Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research.
The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has
hinted
that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been
experimenting
with drug
design
and given Claude a
wet lab
, while OpenAI has been
mowing down
an
impressive
amount
of
longstanding
problems
in
mathematics
and
related fields
.

Adobe’s AI experiments let you walk around in photos and interview your characters
Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.﻿
Here are some of the experimental ‘sneaks’ being showcased at Adobe Max.﻿
by
Jess Weatherbed
Nov 11, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Gift
Project Screen Test lets you talk with AI-generated characters to shape their personality.
Image: Adobe
Jess Weatherbed
is a news writer focused on creative industries, computing, and internet culture. Jess started her career at TechRadar, covering news and hardware reviews.
Some of the most impressive tech that Adobe showcases at its annual Max conference each year is the experimental features it’s developing, and the latest of those tools are being announced today: they can transform images into explorable 3D scenes, design AI characters by talking to them, and turn photo editing into a copy/paste process.
The first (and weirdest, in my opinion) is Project Screen Test, which is designed to make AI-generated characters easier to develop and use for video content. Instead of just describing how the character should sound and behave in text prompts, the tool lets you talk to the character and direct them in an audition-like environment. You start by describing some base personality traits, such as “anxious, shy, awkward,” and giving the character a voice, either by selecting a preset, describing how it sounds in a prompt, or uploading sample audio for it to reference.
You can then expand its persona in further detail by conversing with the character as if you’re talking on FaceTime, outlining its backstory, temperament, goals, flaws, fears, movement quirks and more. Once you’re happy, the tool lets you generate animated screen tests with the character by describing an environment or scenario you want to put them in.
This Personality tab lets you manually adjust any of the traits that were generated for the character by talking to it.
Image: Adobe
This is currently a standalone creative exercise, and it’s not clear how (or if) it could feature in any of Adobe’s existing AI video tools. The results provided a more identifiable and consistent personality compared to many soulless animated AI characters I’ve seen, but that’s the entire reason this exists — AI video generation provides
far
less creative control compared to traditional animation, where every aspect of a character is included with absolute intention.
There’s also Project Sight Span, which reframes photographs and images by turning them into a 3D environment that you can navigate through and reposition. The 3D space generates objects and backgrounds that are outside of the original frame, but feel like a natural part of the image, even if you’re turning to see what’s behind you. While the visuals in the 3D environment are pixelated and ill–defined, the resolution quality is restored when you select your chosen angle.
This still doesn’t really do Project Sight Span justice, but a video demonstration should take place at the Adobe Max sneaks keynote.
Image: Adobe
Sight Span works with any flat image, including photos, paintings, and illustrations, and can preserve and replicate artistic styles. Even repositioned tattoos and facial features in photographs remain surprisingly recognizable and true to the original reference. It’s a bit like a version of
Apple’s Spatial Reframing feature
on steroids: you can reposition more aggressively and change the shooting point entirely if you want, but it also feels far less deserving of being called a photo afterward.
Project Sound Bender is an AI audio mixing feature that lets you customize sound effects as if you’re clicking your cursor around a color wheel. It works by uploading a video clip and then describing your desired audio in a text prompt, such as “bubbling sci-fi cauldron noises.” Sound Bender then generates sound effects and automatically syncs it to the video, and provides a square sound canvas that lets you adjust the noises in real time. Each corner of the canvas will automatically assign a relevant AI-generated sound, such as dense gurgling with popping bubbles, rumbling boiling rocks, pitched bloops, and crackling electric fire. You can drag your cursor around the canvas to select which noises stand out the most, or customize each corner with different sound effects.
Dragging your cursor around that square on the left changes the AI-generated audio as you’re listening to it.
Image:
Adobe also showcased Project Rinse Repeat, which lets you copy edits and then automatically apply them to other objects or people in the same photo. For example, if you painstakingly airbrush out acne or blemishes on one person, Rinse Repeat will adapt your specific changes to anyone else in a group of people who need similar touchups. It can also be used to add shadows to products in marketing graphics, even if the objects are different shapes and sizes. Rinse Repeat is built around Photoshop, and the edits you apply to other subjects remain fully editable because the tool recreates them with native Photoshop tools.
Only one shadow was manually added in this example…
Image: Adobe
…with shadows then added to the remaining products by copy/pasting the process.
Image: Adobe
These “sneaks” are tech previews of capabilities that
might
eventually be developed into tools for Adobe’s Creative Cloud apps or Firefly platform, so there’s no guarantee that they’ll graduate into being available features. Almost all of these projects are built around Adobe’s generative AI developments, however, and given AI tools now play a central role in the company’s growth strategy, it’s likely that at least some of the experiments will see an official launch. As wacky or fun as these AI experiments are, they’re also an omen. If they’re useful enough, that means AI may eventually replace the tools and stock libraries that creative professionals currently use, regardless of how complex their feelings are about the technology.
A notable theme across these sneaks is making complicated photo editing, filmmaking, and audio mixing workflows feel more accessible and intuitive, adapting them into something that’s more interactive and easy to use. In some cases the features almost seem like toys, but with the benefit of allowing you to make practical changes to creative projects.
“Making these interactions more intuitive is also about giving experienced creatives more precise control,” senior principle Adobe research scientist Gautham Mysore, told
The Verge
. “Sound Bender’s sonic exploration capability and Sight Span’s camera positioning are examples of how professionals could apply their judgment and refine a result more directly. That connection between creative intent and control is a big part of what we’re exploring.”
