articles.content:
Title: My AI Agents (Re)discovered a Maya Site in 72 Hours

URL Source: https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site

Final URL: https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site/

Markdown Content:
5 min read (Last edit: 11 Nov)

_Update (11 November): it turns out the site had already been mapped in [Estrada-Belli et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2025.105288). The agents missed it while going through the literature, so they rediscovered it rather than discovered it (it just wasn't in the register of Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History, INAH, yet). Still work to do then! The rest of the story still holds._

By analyzing NASA lidar data, my AI agents found a Maya site in Mexico that wasn't in the official register. (It turned out archaeologists had mapped it already, more on that at the end.) It took **less than 72 hours** to go from a random thought while traveling to an official reply from the Mexican government. This is by far the best time ever to be alive.

Lidar: bare ground, 2013

Satellite image today

**Drag the slider.** The same hilltop today from a satellite (just trees) and in lidar (no trees). Colours show height. Satellite © Esri, Maxar, Earthstar Geographics.

_Disclaimer: I'm not an archaeologist._

I'm going to tell this story as a diary, because the timeline is probably the best part.

## 18 October

I was traveling in Peru, Gemini-ing about the history of the place, when I learned about [Hiram Bingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiram_Bingham_III), the American explorer who "discovered" [Machu Picchu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machu_Picchu) in 1911. "What luck!" I thought. He was actually looking for a different city, [Vilcabamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vilcabamba,_Peru), the last refuge of the Incas, when a local farmer in the valley below guided him to the ruins. "Imagine if Bingham had our tools," I thought. "What would he do?"

**Left:** Bingham at his tent, 1912. **Right:** Machu Picchu, photographed by Bingham the same year. Public domain, Wikimedia Commons ([left](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Hiram_Bingham_at_Machu_Picchu,_1912.jpg), [right](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Machupicchu_hb10.jpg)).

I brainstormed a bit with a few agents (Gemini, ChatGPT, Claude and Grok), and they all said [lidar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lidar). From above, a ruin in the jungle is just a bunch of trees (like Machu Picchu before it was cleared), so satellite photos don't help much. Lidar, instead, fires laser pulses through the gaps in the canopy and maps the ground underneath.[[1]](https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site/#fn-lidar)

So the agents went looking for lidar data. Peru isn't well covered, and hiring a company to do a survey meant permits, costs and bureaucracy, so I gave up on that. Then I thought: why not the [Maya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization)? Their region is much better covered by public lidar.

That night, I asked the agents to analyze it and went to bed.

## 19 October

I woke up and checked the agents' reports. 'DAMN!' They had found lots of villages and other regular shapes that looked like structures or houses.

A few of the sites the agents flagged overnight. Keep an eye on the bottom-left one.

**So how did they do it?** They turned the lidar strips (about 1,200 km² of jungle) into images, and 48 agents went through them one by one like very patient archaeologists, looking for pyramids, platforms, and plazas while filtering out natural hills, sinkholes, and roads. There was no special model or classifier involved: the agents literally looked at the pictures, following a precise guide.

> **Me:** That's awesome! Please check which of these villages haven't been discovered yet. Search both the literature and the archives.
>
>
> _…a few hours later…_
>
>
> **Agent:** One major village doesn't seem to have been registered.

This is the hilltop from the top of this post. It sits on the edge of a cliff, under the jungle, and it has straight edges and sharp corners. Nature doesn't really do straight lines.

Zooming in, there's a levelled plaza, an oval pyramid at least 8–12 m tall, a raised courtyard attached to it and a flat-bottomed hollow that might have been a water reservoir.

The hilltop with the trees removed (top), and a zoom into its civic centre (bottom).

And this is what it looks like in 3D.

The site in 3D, from the lidar. Heights exaggerated ~1.5×.

> **Me:** OK, what should I do?
>
>
> **Agent:** You should contact [INAH](https://www.inah.gob.mx/) (Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History), write a report on your discovery, and check whether the site is in their register. Sometimes they have unpublished results.
>
>
> **Me:** OK, how do I contact INAH? How does the reporting process work?
>
>
> **Agent:**_…instructions for the report… + email addresses_
>
>
> **Me:** OK, please do the report.

And I went to bed.

## 20 October

I iterated on the report a bit, since a few things were off, and translated it into Spanish to improve the chances of getting a reply (at least, that's what Claude suggested). I don't speak Spanish, so I had to trust the agents on that one.

The agents also checked the raw point cloud, to make sure the shapes were really on the ground and not created by the trees. Green dots are leaves, brown dots are the ground.

Two slices through the raw lidar points. Under 10–17 m of forest, the ground (brown) traces the plaza, the pyramid and the courtyard.

Then I sent the report to INAH.

The top of my letter to INAH. The exact coordinates went in a confidential annex, not shown here.

## 21 October

INAH replied: they checked their records and found **no registered archaeological site at that location**.

INAH's reply. The highlighted part: _"…no registered archaeological site was identified at the location given in your report."_

At that point I thought nobody had put it on a map before. I was wrong (see below).

## So what was it?

This part is speculation, from a long chat with the agents. It looks like a small Maya civic centre from the Classic period (roughly AD 250–900), basically the "downtown" of a local elite. The plaza is where people gathered, for ceremonies and maybe even a market. The pyramid was probably a temple, and the raised courtyard next to it might have been where the local ruler lived. The hollow could have been an _aguada_, a rainwater reservoir: Maya towns needed them to get through the dry season. Or it's just a hole. The three platforms around were probably houses.

I asked Gemini to imagine how it looked back then:

How it might have looked around AD 700. Generated with Gemini from the lidar layout

For similar studies, have a look at how NASA's G-LiHT instrument works ([Cook et al. 2013](https://doi.org/10.3390/rs5084045)) and how lidar collected for environmental research can be reused for archaeology ([Golden et al. 2016](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2016.07.029)). In 2024, archaeologists found a whole Maya city in Mexico this way ([Auld-Thomas et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.15184/aqy.2024.148)), others mapped settlements across the Maya lowlands, including this very site ([Estrada-Belli et al. 2025](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jasrep.2025.105288)), and another study found what may have been ancient Maya marketplaces ([Šprajc 2026](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0956536126100923)).

## What's next

The site is now in the hands of the people who should have it: Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) and the archaeologists who mapped it first. If anything comes out of it, I'll post an update.

## What I've learned

You can just do things. I'm not an archaeologist, so I didn't know this was supposed to be hard. I just picked an old problem, tried the most obvious thing and threw some compute at it. Being a naive outsider might be a superpower now.

And it turned out professional archaeologists had already mapped the same site. I guess that's a good sign: an outsider with agents ended up in a similar place to the experts.

And I don't think this is really about archaeology. So far, most agentic AI stories have been about coding, math and physics, but it's much more general than that, and I hope this small example makes it a bit more obvious. We are on the brink of a revolution in all the sciences, and the only bottlenecks left will be curiosity and imagination (and compute).

**At this point, we should probably lidar the whole planet and let the agents discover the rest.**

1.   If you don't know how lidar works, copy and paste this prompt into your favorite AI tool: "Build an HTML page that explains how lidar works, with beautiful visualizations." [↩](https://pietromiotti.com/latest/maya-site/#fr-lidar-1)

Title: United Airlines bans AI agents from booking flights on behalf of travelers

URL Source: https://www.cbsnews.com/news/united-airlines-bans-ai-agents-booking-flights/

Markdown Content:
By

Megan Cerullo is a New York-based reporter for CBS MoneyWatch covering small business, workplace, health care, consumer spending and personal finance topics. She regularly appears on CBS News 24/7 to discuss her reporting.

November 11, 2026 / 2:37 PM EST / MoneyWatch

United Airlines said on Wednesday that it is banning artificial intelligence agents from making flight reservations on behalf of travelers, citing[security risks](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/ai-agents-customer-bank-accounts-security/)and the possibility that such actions could violate federal rules.

Many consumers are turning to AI agents such as [Meta's Muse](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/meta-ai-agent-muse-shopping/)and [OpenAI's dots](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/sam-altman-openai-dots-chatgpt-agents-safety/)to complete tasks ranging from researching products and tracking down deals to making purchases.

To make an airline booking, an AI agent requires access to a customer's personal information, including credentials like payment information. United has a problem with that, saying that "sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles."

The carrier also said that using an AI agent to, for example, check in for a flight could violate federal regulations, including rules requiring travelers to verify in person that their luggage does not contain banned substances.

"As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants," said the airline, which is updating its booking and ticketing policies to reflect the new rule.

United's new policy suggests the company wants to retain control over the customer booking process, said Henry Harteveldt, an aviation analyst at Atmosphere Research Group.

"United is saying they don't want to add yet another, and potentially even more powerful, intermediary than they already face in terms of Google search, price-comparison metasearch sites and online travel agencies," he told CBS News. "Flight searches cost airlines money, and undoubtedly United wants to avoid the expense associated with the surge of AI bot flight searches."

Other airlines are taking a different tack to the emergence of AI agents. For example, Southwest has made its flight inventory viewable to ChatGPT users, who can access the airline's website through the AI app.

United fares will continue to be bookable through flight aggregators such as Kayak, Hopper and Google Flights, Harteveldt said, adding that "consumers shouldn't find it any more difficult to find good fares on the airline."

"But by blocking the AI bots, United won't make it any easier to find its fares, either," he said.

Edited by [Alain Sherter](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/alain-sherter/)

[Kris Van Cleave](https://www.cbsnews.com/team/kris-van-cleave/) contributed to this report.

Title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine

URL Source: https://blog.atuin.sh/threads-agent-sessions/

Published Time: 2026-10-27T19:23:24.000Z

Markdown Content:
> Atuin Threads: one searchable, synced history for every agent session, on every machine
> Start a task in Claude Code, then resume it in Codex on another machine — with all context intact. Install, then run `atuin resume`

0:00

/0:13

Over the past year or two, how I use my terminal has changed dramatically. For years I was the sole user of my shell, and everything in my Atuin history was authored by me. Now, more than half the commands running on my machines weren’t written by me.

These days, much of my work happens through a coding agent, typed into a little “Topsy-turvying” text box. But while my shell history follows me everywhere, my agent sessions do not. They're scattered across different tools and machines (a laptop, a dev server, ephemeral instances on [exe.dev](https://exe.dev/?ref=blog.atuin.sh), a surprisingly cheap bare metal box in Germany), difficult to search, and often forgotten once I've moved on.

It’s a familiar problem!

I started working on Atuin because the history of my work was ephemeral: every command I typed was destined to vanish on line 501 of `.bash_history`. But once this work became indexed, everlasting, and easy to recall, I could find the exact command I’d used to fix something years ago, in seconds.

Over the years, this data compounded. It became the history of all of my work, the record of how I solved problems and built things.

Shell history has always been an excellent record of what happened, but it’s only the surface. It never kept the reasoning… or the intentions behind what I was trying to do. I could only find a command if I remembered a part of it, though often I remembered what I was trying to achieve more readily.

Agent sessions store the lot of it. Every command, its output, my intent, and everything I tried along the way to the eventual solution. It’s all there, in plain English, in my home directory! But just as with shell history all those years ago, we don’t put it to work.

### Atuin Threads

That is why we built Atuin Threads.

Starting with Atuin 18.24, you can search your agent sessions across machines, resume them anywhere, or fork the session into a different agent harness. Start something in Claude Code on a dev server, then finish it in Codex on your laptop.

Behind the scenes, this was a natural extension of Atuin. We put a lot of time and effort into building a reliable, encrypted sync engine. It’s generic, and can sync anything that can be modelled as an append-only log. As it turns out, most AI sessions are exactly this.

Like shell history, Threads is end-to-end encrypted when synced, so we can't read your sessions. You can use our hosted sync server, [run your own](https://docs.atuin.sh/latest/self-hosting/server-setup/?ref=blog.atuin.sh), or keep everything local. Capturing agent sessions is opt-in, too.

Run `atuin resume`, and after setting up, you will see the TUI from the top of this post!

It doesn’t matter which agent you started with - you can resume it anywhere. With Atuin’s sync, this works across devices, and keeps your history backed up forever.

Right now, we support

*   Claude Code
*   Codex
*   Pi
*   Omp
*   OpenCode

with more agents coming soon.

### MCP

With MCP, agents can search and reference previous sessions themselves. They can find work you’ve done before, understand why a decision was made, and build on previous investigations without having to dig up the context.

Our MCP is available as `atuin mcp`, and can be automatically installed with

```
atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode
```

There are all sorts of ways to put this history to work. A few examples:

#### Work that never shipped

I’ve iterated on our onboarding and setup so many times over the past few months, but never quite been happy with it. When I ask an agent to work on onboarding now, it finds all my previous attempts, as well as why they had been abandoned and what can be done better.

These sessions contain the code that never made it into `main`, as well as my initial prompts and iteration. Subsequent agents can use this to figure out exactly what I want, without me having to write up a giant spec.

#### Object store outage

With all the security issues going on in the industry recently, we rolled our keys as a precaution. One of the new object store keys did not have the correct permissions for avatar uploads! We didn’t notice straight away 😬

My daily Sentry triage agent picked up on it, and traced the failure down to a command run earlier that day. I hadn’t gotten around to reading it yet, but prompting another agent with

> seeing some tigris avatar issues?

led to the agent discovering the previous investigation, highlighting the cause, and developing the fix much faster than if it had done the whole thing from scratch.

#### Forking threads across machines

Before releasing Threads, I did some testing on a variety of machines and setups.

One machine did not perform well. The agent investigating proposed that this was because of poor IO performance, but that it needed something with a faster disk to confirm.

I forked the session onto my MacBook, and it continued from exactly where it left off. With the faster SSD, the investigation concluded that slow disk was only part of the story - we could speed up imports elsewhere, too.

Once the benchmarks were complete, the thread running on the original machine could pull the results from the Mac and build a fix. I didn’t have to copy-paste anything or co-ordinate across machines, and the data is now part of the record of my work.

### Teams

While this is tremendously useful as a solo engineer, it gets even more interesting with a team.

So much of what we do never makes it into Git, issue trackers, or documentation. The context behind that work ends up scattered across individual agent sessions. What if the rest of the team could learn from it too? What if we could hand off an agent thread just like a Git branch?

We’re building opt-in session sharing for teams, and would love to hear from folks using agents day to day. If this sounds useful to you, [please get in touch](mailto:ellie@atuin.sh)!

While agents have radically changed my daily workflow, shell history isn’t going anywhere, and is arguably more useful than ever. Threads is an extension of the same idea that started Atuin in the first place - the history of your work should be useful, accessible, and yours to keep.

Threads is out in Atuin 18.24+

1.   Install or update Atuin with `curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -LsSf https://setup.atuin.sh | sh`
2.   Run `atuin resume` to get started
3.   Use the MCP with `atuin mcp install`

Please don’t hesitate to reach out with any questions or feedback!

Title: Your Retirement Savings Are Fueling the AI Bubble

URL Source: https://lpeproject.org/blog/your-retirement-savings-are-fueling-the-ai-bubble/

Published Time: 2026-11-09T11:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Lenore Palladino ([@lenorepalladino](https://twitter.com/lenorepalladino)) is an associate professor of economics and public policy at the University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

Are we on the brink of the next financial crisis? Last Thursday, there was a “[bloodbath in tech stocks](https://ep.ft.com/permalink/emails/eyJlbWFpbCI6ImMzNTQwYzhkNzBlYjZjZmJiYzdiZmI2NDk2N2EyMTQyZjU4OTUzODMwYjk3MTE5YjUyIiwgInRyYW5zYWN0aW9uSWQiOiI5OTdmZDZlOC02ZTlmLTQ5ZWEtYTRhZS00ZTE3MTA0NjY4MjAiLCAiYmF0Y2hJZCI6ImNkZjdmZTcyLWM5OWItNDAyYy1hZWZmLWEyMTUxZmE2NmU1ZSJ9),” as the stock market [lost $3.2 trillion in a single day](https://giftarticle.ft.com/giftarticle/actions/redeem/97949838-0059-421c-8eb9-a2f5ed861747). The media is blaming the “blue wave,” but anxiety about the AI boom was already rising before the election. The week prior, on October 29, the “Magnificent Seven”—the tech companies that have driven much of the stock market’s recent growth—[lost nearly a trillion dollars](https://giftarticle.ft.com/giftarticle/actions/redeem/3f58ba03-b109-4c6c-9581-8623ed87eb37) in value. The immediate catalyst for that sell-off was the realization that Google, Amazon, and Meta have all become “[cash incinerators](https://giftarticle.ft.com/giftarticle/actions/redeem/3f58ba03-b109-4c6c-9581-8623ed87eb37),” as their latest earnings reports showed [astronomical spending on AI](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/29/technology/amazon-earnings-tech-spending.html) and a [growing reliance on borrowing](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-28/wall-street-s-ai-debt-machine-is-starting-to-choke-on-supply?leadSource=uverify%20wall). The question that skeptics have long raised about the data center buildout has suddenly reached a fever pitch: will there actually be enough demand for AI for the companies to cover these massive investments and pay back their loans?

What has yet to enter public consciousness, however, is the extent to which working people’s financial assets have been used to fuel this bubble. Individuals protesting data centers often have no idea that their retirement accounts are being used to finance the companies responsible for these projects. Nor are they aware that they are at risk of being left holding the bag.

As “private” credit and equity funds have become [a new center of gravity](https://phenomenalworld.org/analysis/finance-in-the-dark/) in financial markets, our public pension fund systems have increasingly allocated [the retirement savings of public sector workers](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/10957960261472463) to these opaque, [unregulated institutions](https://lpeproject.org/blog/private-financial-markets-are-eating-the-world/). Similarly, thanks to [recent efforts](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/08/democratizing-access-to-alternative-assets-for-401k-investors/) by the Trump administration, the [$15 trillion](https://www.ici.org/statistical-report/ret_26_q2) held in private sector workers’ retirement accounts is now, for the first time in history, [available to be invested in private funds](https://www.dollarsandsense.org/retirement-savings-in-the-dark/). And it is to these funds that the companies building out data centers (and the [gas plants necessary to power them](https://lpeproject.org/blog/the-neoliberal-grid-is-in-crisis/)) have turned for financing. According to a [new report from Americans for Financial Reform](https://ourfinancialsecurity.org/resources/tracing-the-money-private-equity-and-data-centers/), for instance, private equity firms are behind 25-30% of data center financing. By putting our retirement chips in their basket, we are bound up in the risks that these companies are taking in the AI boom—even though they do not have to disclose those risks to us.

What are those risks? While the AI bubble is not, thankfully, built on an edifice of predatory mortgages, the complexity and scale of the loans made to data center operators and Big Tech is giving many people painful flashbacks to 2008. As the credit ratings agency S&P stated plainly in September, “[the credit quality of hyperscalers is weakening,](https://readwise.io/reader/shared/01m2kf1v0c2hk6yftmsyprms2t)” due to the projected $7 trillion in spending by 2030, much of which has to be financed by debt. That deterioration is already appearing in credit markets. Sales of the [infamous credit default swaps](https://www.ft.com/content/67da8e84-17b3-4371-a1f8-2fbe02997491) (CDS) are [quickly increasing](https://www.ft.com/content/6dd31584-064c-4015-bf5d-e5747799ccd5?syn-25a6b1a6=1): more than $9 billion of CDS linked to Big Tech bonds was traded weekly in September, and they’re getting more expensive as there is more demand for the protection they offer. All of the financial transactions involved in building data centers are also increasingly correlated due to the [dense web of financing and customer relationships](https://www.bis.org/publications/bulletin-137-circular-relationships-among-ai-firms.pdf) in the sector, as well as the complexity of financing relationships in many data center projects. As [S&P states](https://readwise.io/reader/shared/01m2kf1v0c2hk6yftmsyprms2t), “if demand disappoints, chip values fall, or data center utilization declines, do the losses sit with the operator, the sponsor or the guarantor?”

These risks are complicated by last week’s election. Voters overwhelmingly rejected the construction of data centers—electing governors in [Texas,](https://ginafortexas.com/priority/data-centers/)[Georgia](https://atlantadailyworld.com/2026/09/12/keisha-lance-bottoms-calls-for-pause-on-new-data-centers-rick-jackson-is-forcing-them-onto-communities/), and [New Mexico](https://debhaaland.com/2026/09/haaland-backs-data-center-moratorium-outlines-accountability-plan-to-stand-up-for-new-mexicos-water-and-communities/?srsltid=AYCX9vJ_iMRqGZuqMxUAz2Uy3i2hmEcmPZYA0m-2YINWslOL_-oATE6m) who have committed to some form of data center slowdown or moratorium, while approving nearly every [ballot measure that called for data center moratoria or slowdowns](https://datacentersontheballot.com/). According to Axios, Texas was projected to account for [nearly half of the data center buildout in 2028](https://www.axios.com/2026/11/04/ai-data-center-election-slowdown?__readwiseLocation=). Gina Hinojosa’s victory over Greg Abbott just changed the whole trajectory of the industry. Elon Musk, as the results came in, [observed](https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2117862462976594112) that “data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.” This is an excellent outcome—not least because it may prompt some companies to revise their projected data center buildout—yet it does not wipe away the mountain of debt that has already accumulated, nor the risk that these debts will become unpayable.

The [risk of financial collapse](https://www.openmarketsinstitute.org/publications/report-brace-for-impact-protecting-people-and-the-economy-when-the-ai-bubble-burst) is not, at the end of the day, the [most damaging part](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/19/big-tech-vowed-lead-climate-now-its-driving-fossil-fuel-boom/) of the AI buildout. Yet it is the aspect over which pension fund trustees and people saving for retirement have the most control—we can demand that our pensions refrain from holding risky, unregulated financial assets linked to the data center boom, as [some public pension fund trustees](https://www.wsj.com/finance/investing/politicians-are-turning-against-ai-but-your-pension-is-riding-on-it-6764d852) have started to do. Employees can demand that their employer find an asset manager that will not move their funds into unregulated financial assets. Note, however, that this will require more than shifting our portfolios “back” towards holding index funds that buy the tech-heavy stock market. As SpaceX becomes part of the S&P 500, and Anthropic and OpenAI become publicly traded, the stock markets will only get more AI-pilled.

In the longer term, with enough political will, we can redirect our retirement savings towards productive investment, such as [building out affordable housing](https://ourfinancialsecurity.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/AffordableHousing_final_web-1.pdf) and funding the renewable energy transition. For example, NYC Comptroller Mark Levine [announced a $4 billion affordable housing initiative](https://comptroller.nyc.gov/newsroom/nyc-comptroller-mark-levine-launches-the-nyc-housing-investment-initiative-a-4-billion-commitment-to-finance-housing-across-five-boroughs/) in April. Pension fund trustees could follow his lead rather than direct money towards Blackstone, [one of the country’s largest landlords](https://www.banking.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/20260325_letter_to_blackstone_re_institutional_investors_housingpdf.pdf) and a major fund manager for public pensions. More ambitiously, as I’ve written elsewhere, the government should [establish public asset managers](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00346764.2023.2237485) and a [public credit fund](https://doi.org/10.1080/08911916.2026.2730245) to change the structure of how public pension funds are deployed. We do not need to act as if pension funds and retirement accounts are being directed into the AI bubble by the invisible hand of the market: portfolio allocation choices are, in the context of this complicated disaster, some of the easiest places to apply pressure.

Recently, Michael Burry, the hedge fund manager made famous by Michael Lewis’ _The Big Short_, [said](https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2026-ai-data-center-build-costs/?accessToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzb3VyY2UiOiJTdWJzY3JpYmVyR2lmdGVkQXJ0aWNsZSIsImlhdCI6MTc5MzYyMjU5MCwiZXhwIjoxNzk0MjI3MzkwLCJhcnRpY2xlSWQiOiJUTVNJSUVLSUpIQTgwMCIsImJjb25uZWN0SWQiOiJBM0Q0RTc1NzMyRTE0MkE3OEI3OUU5NDI2NTdGQTYwNCJ9.cbaBbhh7DK2UfI7szLbfj9iDsVifcdif1O4427IkgMM) “all the capital being spent and lent by the richest companies on Earth won’t be enough to keep the bubble from eventually bursting.” One of the most galling claims after the Great Financial Crisis was that no one could have seen it coming. This time, at least, it is staring us right in the face.

URL Source: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811

Markdown Content:
**[Hacker News](https://news.ycombinator.com/news)**[new](https://news.ycombinator.com/newest) | [past](https://news.ycombinator.com/front) | [comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/newcomments) | [ask](https://news.ycombinator.com/ask) | [show](https://news.ycombinator.com/show) | [jobs](https://news.ycombinator.com/jobs) | [submit](https://news.ycombinator.com/submit)[login](https://news.ycombinator.com/login?goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811)

[Launch HN: Pomerado (YC F26) – Turn any website into an MCP for agents](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811) 48 points by [alanjm23](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=alanjm23)[9 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811) | [hide](https://news.ycombinator.com/hide?id=50455811&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811) | [past](https://hn.algolia.com/?query=Launch%20HN%3A%20Pomerado%20%28YC%20F26%29%20%E2%80%93%20Turn%20any%20website%20into%20an%20MCP%20for%20agents&type=story&dateRange=all&sort=byDate&storyText=false&prefix&page=0) | [favorite](https://news.ycombinator.com/fave?id=50455811) | [40 comments](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811) Hi HN, we’re Alan and Akshay from Pomerado ([https://pomerado.ai/](https://pomerado.ai/)). We connect your agents to any website by turning sites into deterministic, self-healing APIs in minutes, fully self-serve. Agents are no longer limited by their intelligence, but rather by their ability to interact with systems. Airlines, banks, e-commerce, insurance portals, government sites, and legacy portals all lack APIs or MCPs and are common parts of personal assistant or business workflows. Agents instead rely on browser automation or computer use, which can be slow, expensive, and unreliable. And even if computer use were perfect, most companies have banned it out of security and compliance concerns. We discovered this problem while tinkering with our own personal assistants. When OpenClaw came out, we wanted to “live our lives through our agents” and have them do everything for us. We soon found their usefulness was restricted by what tools they could connect to. For example, when trying to book flights, they fell back on computer use, which failed to checkout. These issues got magnified on repeated workflows, like searching many airlines at once. Pomerado started off as a project to improve these personal assistant workflows. As we started building, we realized that just-in-time tool creation could have significant applications for AI builders in legacy verticals. We’re ex-McKinsey and Scale AI, where we drove agent deployments in healthcare, professional services, and telecom. Each time, the biggest bottleneck was getting agents to interface well with legacy websites and apps. Pomerado is what we built. It’s a self-serve platform where devs can create APIs for any website (even those they don’t own), in minutes. Users (or their coding agents) provide a short natural language description, answer a few questions about their workflow, and receive a MCP in less than an hour. Future tool calls use the deterministic MCP, which usually returns results in 5-30 seconds. Here’s a walkthrough of our product: [https://youtu.be/Bi4jci7rgHo](https://youtu.be/Bi4jci7rgHo) In practice: - Our agent opens a browser, explores the website, and performs the requested task once by writing HTTP requests or a Playwright script. This example run establishes how to navigate the website, interact with the relevant controls, and obtain the desired result. If any additional user input is needed (e.g., login, clarification) the agent will ask the user over MCP. - Afterwards, the agent uses the example run, along with all of the data it recorded, to create a generalizable and repeatable API. Throughout this process, a separate Guardian model reviews the coding agent’s calls against a set of guardrails. We also run a battery of tests with synthetic inputs to ensure that the API is generalized and not overfit to one input. A final publication agent ensures that the integration publishes a reasonable and generalized input/output schema - We also handle sites that require authentication and 2FA. For authentication, we pass off to a deterministic sign-in process to ensure the model and our recorders never read customer credentials. Users can store 2FA TOTP seeds or link their account to a Pomerado phone number for us to autofill 2FA for them as well - If future runs fail, a maintenance job is kicked off to repair and improve the tool. The maintenance job can fix broken steps (e.g., a renamed button), add additional functionality (e.g., searching for business class flights in addition to economy), or add new guardrails (e.g., reservation dates must be in the future). We’ve even seen people improve tools by just saying “please make this faster” Unlike computer use, our MCPs are deterministic at runtime, which makes them much faster and cheaper. By taking slightly longer to do a task the first time, you reap the benefits much more in the future. It’s a great fit for repeated, high-volume tasks you want your agent to do. We’d love to have you try it! We have both an open-source (MIT) ([https://github.com/Pomerado/pomerado](https://github.com/Pomerado/pomerado)) and a free hosted version ([https://app.pomerado.ai](https://app.pomerado.ai/)). So far, users of Pomerado include: - A personal trainer using agents to prepare workouts and message clients. Before Pomerado, agents couldn’t login and use the site reliably, so this was all manual - Car dealerships connecting their Grok Bots to legacy dealer systems, including marketplaces, CRMs, and ERPs. Dealers switched from computer use, which could take 1hr+ - Personal assistants using Pomerado to integrate with a broad range of consumer websites Please ask any questions or share any feedback in the comments, thanks! [help](https://news.ycombinator.com/formatdoc) [rahimnathwani](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=rahimnathwani)[8 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50456440) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50461281)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) What are the main advantages compared with [https://github.com/mvanhorn/cli-printing-press](https://github.com/mvanhorn/cli-printing-press) The obvious differences I can see are: - generates an MCP server instead of a CLI - at 'minting' time, uses OpenAI API keys, instead of coding agent subscription - tries to solve for a particular use case, instead of all the site provides [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50456440&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811%2350456440) [am03](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=am03)[8 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50456925) | [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50456440) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50461281)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Printing Press is a great project! At a philosophical level, Pomerado is meant to be more autonomous - it's a standalone harness that you can run, and it's meant to require as little review as possible after the first request. If there are questions about the site or intent, we have coding agents with application context answer those questions. We find this integrates into automated software development workflows a lot better, and my Openclaw can basically create new MCPs for me with little supervision required. In terms of mechanisms, Pomerado uses a mix of HTTP requests and generated Playwright code. Printing Press has a far greater emphasis on making HTTP requests to the site's backend. We've found for some sites this latter approach can create issues around triggering anti-bot and can fail for more complicated forms and writes, so we use Playwright for those instances. Pomerado's approach to researching the website is also a bit different - we solely focus on exploring the website itself, while Printing Press has your agent explore the web for documentation, SDKs, etc. There's a tradeoff of prompt injection security vs convenience there. Because we try to emphasize autonomous builds we limit the agent to the website for security. A big pain point for us with existing approaches was using them for cloud agents (e.g., my Openclaw on my VPS). Cloud starts running into a lot of issues around hosting, authentication, and anti-bot, which is why we started offering a free hosted version of the open source, where we handle cloud browsers, proxy rotation, credential storage, CAPTCHAs, etc. We're planning to roll out support for CLIs down the line! And the PR for non-OpenAI models + codex exec is in the works :) [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50456925&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811%2350456925) [jeroenhd](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=jeroenhd)[2 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50461281) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50456440) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50457395)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Do you respect the wishes of sites and services that do not want the extra load? How does one opt their online service out? [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50461281&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811%2350461281) [bshafiq](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=bshafiq)[7 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50457395) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50461281) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50459667)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Congrats on the launch! The approach of turning unstructured sites into deterministic MCPs is really interesting, especially the self-healing maintenance jobs. Curious about the failure mode: what happens when a browser action fails or times out? The agent will often just blindly retry the exact same MCP tool call with the exact same arguments. Since the tool call itself returns a 200 OK, standard retry counters miss it, and you just burn tokens while the browser keeps timing out in the background. Are you doing any payload/state validation at the runtime layer to hard-stop those cyclic failures before the next call, or does the Guardian model handle that? [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50457395&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811%2350457395) [alanjm23](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=alanjm23)[7 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50457606) | [parent](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50457395) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50459667)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Thanks! When a browser action fails or times out, the repair agent should step in to fix the integration and prevent retries from looping. There are also a few conditions where we automatically kick off a repair without a failing job, such as a streak of rejected inputs or site errors. This is to try and prevent silent failures. [reply](https://news.ycombinator.com/reply?id=50457606&goto=item%3Fid%3D50455811%2350457606) [jrecyclebin](https://news.ycombinator.com/user?id=jrecyclebin)[4 hours ago](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50459667) | [prev](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50457395) | [next](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50455811#50460125)[[–]](javascript:void(0)) Site must be slammed - but I'm interested bc I'm working on a similar thing. But my project (one aspect at least) is for expressing HTTP calls as MCP tools. The format looks like this: ``` --- [add-list-item] Add a new item to a list. # Adjust the fields object to match your list's actual columns. $fields is object POST https://graph.microsoft.com/v1.0/sites/$site_id/lists/$list_id/items Authorization: Bearer $token Content-Type: application/json { "fields": $fields } HTTP 201 ``` Been having a lot of fun with this, as I can pile up these integrations and make detailed MCPs quickly. Title: TinyGPT Visualizer: Tools for Exploring the Souls of Large Language Models

URL Source: https://oshea00.github.io/posts/tinygpt-visualizer/

Published Time: 2026-10-29T00:00:00Z

Markdown Content:
There is that old joke told by Woody Allen describing his experience as a university student: “I was thrown out of college for cheating on the metaphysics exam; I looked into the soul of the boy sitting next to me.” If he’d managed to pass his course, Woody Allen might have been ahead of his time.

Metaphysics is becoming a popular topic today, and it seems now everyone desperately wants to look for souls in large language models (LLMs). A recent conference last April was held by Anthropic with religious scholars and philosophical thinkers to discuss the nature of the soul when it came to their latest Claude models. It seems they needed guidance that Dario Amodei was unable to provide.

The time seems ripe to dig into how we might actually peer into the mind of the LLM sitting next to you. There’s been a lot of ongoing research; however, the self-same foundation model companies, Anthropic and OpenAI among them, have been [criticized](https://www.theinformation.com/newsletters/ai-agenda/openai-anthropic-cap-compute-r-d-say-ai-safety-advocates) for dedicating more compute dollars into better models rather than the safety research. Mechanistic interpretability, the field of AI research devoted to exploring what goes on inside these models, has [grown from a handful of researchers in 2021 to hundreds of active contributors](https://aisecurityandsafety.org/en/guides/mechanistic-interpretability/). Yet, in spite of funding gaps and the lack of larger colloquiums, the research community has been coming up with some interesting insights and tools to help do the “peering.”

Rather than sit on the sidelines and wonder how this could be done, I thought it would be interesting to create a tool that would allow more people to join the party. And that is what led to the development of the “TinyGPT Visualizer.” The goals I had for this were modest. I wanted a tool I could use to survey the field and try the actual techniques to learn how they work. Being a visual person, I began thinking about an X-ray machine—something able to see inside a real model. Not a toy model. A real one, but one small enough to see on a screen with all its working parts.

Let me show what it looks like:

TinyGPT Visualizer walkthrough: inside the network

We may wonder where the consciousness can be found in the collection of numeric matrices that our models comprise; the numbers are there to see. Unlike the brains of humans, we can stop and look at the numbers as the thoughts are formed without killing the patient, and, unlike human brains, we can search those numbers for patterns and algorithms which explain the results these models emit as well-formed prose, code, music, and videos. Will we find well-formed emotions? If so, they will be in the numbers.

Will philosophy and religion help us? These disciplines haven’t had to rely on numbers and calculations up to this point, but perhaps they now have new ground to pound.

TinyGPT Visualizer is open source. You can find the code, setup instructions, and documentation on GitHub: [github.com/oshea00/tinygpt-viz](https://github.com/oshea00/tinygpt-viz).

Title: Modern Web Guidance 1.0: The web platform expertise your coding agent is missing  |  Blog  |  Chrome for Developers

URL Source: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/modern-web-guidance-v1

Markdown Content:
Published: November 10, 2026

In this new era of agentic web development, developers _expect_ their coding agents to be experts at building for the web. And while the latest frontier coding models are quite capable and can usually produce something that works, if you ask a web development expert to review the AI-generated code, they can almost always find ways to make the code faster, more accessible, or more secure.

Chrome is investing heavily in the future of agentic web development, and to address this challenge, we introduced an [early preview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bo3i0FzDUYo) of [Modern Web Guidance](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) at Google I/O in May. Modern Web Guidance is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents.

Today we're excited to announce the stable release of Modern Web Guidance version 1.0, which includes:

*   **New modernization workflow** that scans your existing codebase to help your agent find opportunities to safely modernize.
*   **Expanded guide database** targeting hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps with expert-vetted, cross-browser solutions.
*   **Deeper human expert review** for every guide, including sign-off from content area tech leads and a dedicated accessibility review on our user-facing guides.
*   **Full evaluation coverage** across all of our guides with a [public eval dashboard](https://goo.gle/mwg-evals) showing the measurable improvements compared to agents without Modern Web Guidance.

With version 1.0, we're also excited to share that Modern Web Guidance is becoming a cross-browser effort, with [Firefox and Edge joining Chrome](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/GOVERNANCE.md#owners) to support, improve cross-browser compatibility, and contribute to the project. Building on our shared work with [Baseline](https://web.dev/baseline), our goal is to ensure that anyone coding with an agent can take full advantage of the power and capabilities of the modern web platform.

Regardless of what models or agent harnesses you're using, if you're building for the web, Modern Web Guidance belongs in your agentic workflow.

To install Modern Web Guidance, run this command from your project directory:

```
npx modern-web-guidance@latest install
```

Or if you already installed an earlier version, you can update to 1.0 by running:

```
npx modern-web-guidance@latest update
```

For additional installation instructions or to learn more, check out the [Modern Web Guidance documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance), or watch this video for a brief overview:

## Why developers and businesses should use Modern Web Guidance

It's undeniable that coding agents have helped developers write code faster than ever before. But in a world where everyone is using coding agents, speed is no longer a competitive advantage.

These days, it's more important than ever to differentiate on fundamental factors like usability and quality of experience. Here are a few ways Modern Web Guidance can help:

### Reinforce best practices that models often miss

While frontier coding models do have a good grasp on many best practices, our [evals show](https://goo.gle/mwg-evals) that there are still a number of important areas where they fall short, such as:

*   **Accessibility:** Keyboard focus and inert management, reduced-motion support, and accessible form validation.
*   **User experience:** Swipe and touch gestures, dialog and popover transitions, and light/dark theme implementations.
*   **Performance:** Main-thread task scheduling, offscreen rendering isolation, and layout shift prevention.
*   **Security:** Safe HTML sanitization, strict Content Security Policies, and passkey credential management.

Accessibility best practices are particularly important to get right because mistakes like bad ARIA can make a page less accessible than no ARIA at all. For version 1.0, our user-facing guides were reviewed and tested with real assistive technologies by accessibility experts who rely on them every day.

For a deeper look at the specific mistakes models make in each of these areas, read [Top 10 things AI gets wrong in web development](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/top-10-things-ai-gets-wrong-in-web-dev).

### Use the best web feature for the job

AI models are very good at figuring out how to make something work with JavaScript, but in many cases, there are HTML or CSS features that can do the same thing with much less code. And since they're handled by the browser, they usually perform better and come with accessibility affordances. For example:

*   Features to animate popovers and dialogs
*   Features to enhance scroll- and swipe-based interactions
*   Better APIs for smooth and fluid page transitions

New features can also improve the experience of a site in ways that matter to users. For example:

*   **Passkeys and WebAuthn:** For faster and more secure login experiences
*   **Autofill:** To improve checkout flows (especially on mobile) that often fail when using custom JavaScript-based form controls

Modern Web Guidance is designed to recommend the best feature for the job, based on your browser support requirements. Its guides have embedded Baseline and browser compatibility data, so it can tailor its recommendations to your project's needs.

### Scan your codebase and find opportunities to modernize

Most web development doesn't happen in brand-new projects. It happens in existing codebases that have accumulated years of outdated workarounds, unnecessary dependencies, and polyfills that are no longer needed.

Version 1.0 adds a new [modernization workflow](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance/modernization-workflow) that can analyze your existing HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and `package.json` to find opportunities to safely upgrade, and then guide your agent through the changes.

```
/modern-web-guidance Modernize the code in this directory
```

In this first release, the modernization workflow uses static analysis to check for a limited set of patterns. We chose to start with a narrow scope that yields predictable results, and then expand from there. Over time, we plan to cover many more areas, including agentic audits where your agent reasons about your code directly instead of just matching known patterns.

### Stay up to date as the web platform evolves

The web platform is a moving target. New features ship in browsers every milestone, and existing features that you perhaps couldn't use before are [becoming Baseline](https://web.dev/baseline#the-baseline-monthly-digest) with each new browser release.

Since Modern Web Guidance is built on top of Baseline compatibility data, and its recommendations are maintained by browser engineers, web standards experts, and accessibility specialists, these recommendations evolve along with the platform itself, and now your project can too.

### Learn about new web features and best practices

While Modern Web Guidance is primarily built as a tool for agents, one thing we've heard from many developers is that they've actually found the guidance to be quite useful on its own—as a learning resource.

Even in this era of agentic coding, there's still value in building up domain expertise. And Modern Web Guidance can help you do that: either by reading the guides themselves, or using the CLI to search use cases and discover new techniques that may be relevant to your project.

## Pair Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents

In agentic web development, authoring code is only one part of the workflow. You also need to run that code to ensure it works as expected. This is why we recommend developers use Modern Web Guidance along with [Chrome DevTools for agents](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/agents).

*   **Modern Web Guidance** gives your agent the up-front expertise needed to write code following modern best practices.
*   **Chrome DevTools for agents** gives your agent runtime visibility so it can verify, debug, and optimize that code across a wide range of device capabilities, user preferences, and network conditions.

Together these help your agent arrive at a better solution in fewer turns. Next are a few examples of how you can use these tools together to maximize effectiveness:

### Optimize until you hit your performance target

Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to effectively break up long-running JavaScript tasks that block the main thread, but it can't test your code to see how long those JavaScript tasks actually block the main thread for.

With Chrome DevTools for agents, you can run a performance trace on a simulated low-end CPU to see whether or not you have a problem, and then use the performance advice from Modern Web Guidance to iterate until your code never blocks the main thread for more than 50 milliseconds (so it doesn't contribute to poor INP).

### Test and refine your animations

Modern Web Guidance can show your agent how to properly and performantly animate features like modal dialogs, tooltips, and popover menus, but even with this guidance you still need to verify that the animations actually work and look good when used in the context of your full application.

Chrome DevTools for agents can run your code, interact with the page, and take a screen recording of the animation in action. It can then study the recording to ensure both that the animation runs and that it fits the style and feel of the rest of the site.

You can also use Chrome DevTools for agents to verify that when `prefers-reduced-motion` is set, the component honors the user's preferences.

### Cache views without memory leaks

Modern Web Guidance can teach your agent how to make SPA transitions feel instant by rendering and caching views in memory, while also properly hiding them from the accessibility tree.

However, when doing this it's important to ensure you properly clean up unused views to not leak memory if the user stays on the page for a long time. Chrome DevTools for agents has memory debugging tools, so your agent can ensure memory use isn't increasing without bound.

For a closer look at how to use Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents together, check out this video:

## Success stories

Engineering teams around the world are already using Modern Web Guidance and Chrome DevTools for agents to improve code quality, speed up delivery, and eliminate manual debugging bottlenecks:

### Pensionbazaar and Policybazaar

Pensionbazaar, a new retirement planning platform launched by Indian fintech company Paisabazaar, [paired Modern Web Guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/policybazaar-agentic-audit) to build and verify new pages, shortening turnaround by **more than 90%** (from about four days to a few hours) and reducing UI bugs on new screens by **over 90%**. Its sister platform Policybazaar, one of India's leading insurance platforms with more than 97 million registered customers, used Chrome DevTools for agents to automate performance audits across about 30 high-traffic landing pages, cutting manual auditing effort by **92%**:

> "For Pensionbazaar, our priority was building quality code from day one to avoid technical debt later. Modern Web Guidance steered our coding agent to adopt modern web standards and performance best practices while respecting our specific browser compatibility targets. This made our frontend code reviews substantially easier and faster, ultimately improving our development turnaround time."
>
>
> —**Aman Soni**, Engineering Manager, Policybazaar

articles.content:
Title: GitHub - klad-app/klad: A drawing app built for agent/human collaboration

URL Source: https://github.com/klad-app/klad

Markdown Content:
**Give your agent real brushes.** klad is a 2D painting and animation app you share with a coding agent. You paint in the editor with a pen. The agent paints through the `klad` command line, with the same brushes, on the same drawing, and each of you sees the other's strokes instantly.

_don't want to build it? Sign up for the pre-built app release at [klad.studio](https://klad.studio/)_

**There is no image model in klad.** Your agent (Claude Code, Codex, anything that can run commands) decides what to paint; klad gives it brushes, layers and a timeline. Whatever either of you puts down stays what it was: a stroke with its path, pressure, brush and colour, a shape with its points, a fill with its region. So there's no rerolling and hoping for the best: if one leaf looks off, you fix that leaf.

_Asked for "a little sprout creature for my game", the agent paints 4,344 strokes and fills. You change them: recolour the leaves, bend the mouth, move a smudge, blend the blush. Then the agent animates it: the creature's parts go into five groups, 205 keys move them, and no frame is painted again._

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
|  |  |

_Drawings made with Claude Fable 5.2: the creature, the scene and the prop kit were painted stroke by stroke through the `klad` command line._

*   **Site and guides:**[klad.studio](https://klad.studio/), with these drawings replayed stroke by stroke.
*   **Licence:** source-available, not open source. Free to build and use for yourself, and inside a company with less than 500,000 euros a year in revenue. See [Licence](https://github.com/klad-app/klad#licence).
*   **Runs on:** macOS (pen pressure and tilt). It also builds and passes its tests on Linux and Windows, checked on every change; the editor starts on Linux with the mouse for now, and nobody has drawn with it on Windows yet.
*   **Status:** early. This is the first public version, and you build it yourself: see [From source](https://github.com/klad-app/klad#from-source).

## Why not just generate the picture?

An image generator hands you pixels, and the only edit left is another roll of the dice. klad keeps every stroke and every fill as data: where it went, how hard it was pressed, its brush and its colour. Pick any of them hours later, yours or the agent's, and recolour it, bend it, move it or delete it.

*   **It's paint, not just vectors.** A stroke keeps its path and pressure like a vector does, and still lands as paint. Loaded oil leaves ridges that catch the light, and smudge drags the paint already on the layer. The smudge stays a stroke too: move it later and klad blends it again where it lands.
*   **It can also do just vectors.** Shapes with editable points, gradients, glows and real text in about fifty open fonts that come with it, for posters, covers and cards.
*   **It's a full painting and animation app.** Two dozen brushes and a brush editor, layers, masks, clipping, effects, a timeline with onion skins and clips, in-betweens made from your key drawings, bones with IK, and exports as PNGs, sprite sheets or straight into Godot.
*   **Your drawings stay yours.** A drawing is a folder of plain files on your computer, and klad needs no account. It only looks for a new version once a day, and you can turn that off. An edit changes only the files of what it edits, so drawings live well in git.

## Working with your agent

1.   **Ask.** Tell your agent what the drawing needs, in plain words: a lantern for the inn, lit from the left, on its own layer.
2.   **Watch.** It paints through the `klad` command line, and its strokes show up in your editor about a second later.
3.   **Point.** Pin a note on the canvas or select the part you mean ("more moss on this side"). The agent reads both.
4.   **Take over.** Repaint whatever you like by hand, the agent's strokes as much as your own. Its strokes are marked as its own and every change is one step in a shared history, so you can undo any of it.

The prompt to start with is under [Try it](https://github.com/klad-app/klad#try-it). `klad skill` prints the agent skill in `docs/skill/SKILL.md`: how to look at a drawing, change it and check the result. A second one, `klad skill drawing` (`docs/skill/drawing/SKILL.md`), teaches the craft: planning a picture, light on form, values, edges, colour, materials and how to judge the result. Both are MIT, so use them with any agent and any tool. Open the drawing to watch and draw along:

What an agent paints depends on the agent and on how much you steer it. The skills teach it the tool and some craft; the pen in your hand does the rest.

## For developers: the drawing is data

Everything you can do in the editor has a `klad` command too, so a script or an agent works on the same drawing you have open. It reads strokes as JSON, changes any of them by its address and applies batches of edits as JSON ops.

| To | In the editor | From a script or an agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paint | **B** and a pen with pressure | `klad stroke art.klad l4 --brush oil --path 'M100 400 C 300 200 500 600 700 400'` |
| Change a stroke later | **S** to pick it, then recolour, resize or move; **A** bends its path | `klad set art.klad c4:s12 size=3.5 color=#3355aa` |
| Read what is there | Point at it with **S** | `klad strokes art.klad l4 --json` |
| Flat colour | **G**, filling against the lines layer | `klad fill art.klad l2 --at 820,640 --ref lines --gap 4 --color skin` |
| Point at something | **N** pins a note, **S** selects | `klad notes art.klad`, `klad selection art.klad` |
| In-betweens | The in-between window | `klad inbetween art.klad --layers lines,colour --from 0 --to 6` |
| Export | **cmd E**, or export to Godot from a clip | `klad export art.klad --godot ../game/art` |
| Undo | **cmd Z**, or the History pane | `klad undo art.klad` |

The file format is documented down to the byte under the MIT licence (`docs/format.md`), so other apps and engines can read and write klad drawings with or without klad.

## Made for games

Props, characters, backgrounds and frame-by-frame animation. Draw the key poses and klad makes the drawings in between, part by part; it checks the arcs (a foot that slides, a part that sinks under the ground), colours every drawing from the first one, and exports sprite sheets or a Godot `SpriteFrames` scene with each clip's timing.

klad inbetween creature.klad --layers lines,colour --from 3 --to 5 --spacing in-out
klad arcs creature.klad --track 'lines:near leg' --clip walk --check
klad export creature.klad --godot ../game/art

## Try it

git clone https://github.com/klad-app/klad && cd klad
just compile                  # about ten minutes the first time
target/release/klad open      # on Linux: target/linux/release/klad open

### Then let your agent paint

1.   Put `klad` on your path, for you and for your agent: `target/release/klad install` (on Linux `target/linux/release/klad install`; on a Mac it may ask for your password).

2.   Start your coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, or anything else that can run commands) in the folder where the drawing should go, and paste:

> Run `klad skill` and `klad skill drawing` and read what they print. Then make scene.klad and paint a night scene: a hooded traveller holding a lantern out to a ruined arch, a small creature following, flat shaded and lit by the lantern.

3.   Once it has made `scene.klad`, open it in another terminal to watch the strokes land, and draw along: `klad open scene.klad`.

4.   Then steer it. Press **N** to pin a note on the canvas ("more moss on this side") and tell the agent to read your notes, or pick any stroke with **S** and change it yourself.

Every build holds the `klad` command line tool, the editor, the fonts, the licences, the agent skill and six sample drawings to look at and draw on (the start window shows them; `klad samples` lists them and copies one out). The first start offers first steps: draw a shape, fill it and hand the drawing to an agent. The guides in `docs/guide/` show how to paint, select, fill, animate, rig and export in the editor, one recipe at a time, starting with [Getting started](https://github.com/klad-app/klad/blob/main/docs/guide/getting-started.md).

### From source

Building takes about ten minutes the first time.

1.   Install Rust with [rustup](https://rustup.rs/) and [`just`](https://github.com/casey/just) (`brew install just`, or `cargo install just`). On Linux also `pkg-config`, `libfreetype-dev`, `libfontconfig1-dev`, `libxkbcommon-dev` and `libwayland-dev`.
2.   `git clone https://github.com/klad-app/klad && cd klad`, then `just compile` makes `klad` and `klad-editor` for the machine you are on, in `target/release/` (on Linux in `target/linux/release/`). What you build is for your own use, or your company's if it had less than 500,000 euros in revenue last year (see [Licence](https://github.com/klad-app/klad#licence)).
3.   `target/release/klad open` starts the editor on its start window: make a drawing and start painting, or take first steps (Help > First steps in the editor).
4.   `target/release/klad install` puts `klad` on your terminal's path, for you and for agents (the editor's document menu has the same as "install the klad command").
5.   `just samples` builds the sample drawings in `samples/` (a lantern, a walking creature, a running courier, an underground ruin, an inn sign, a tree, a meadow, painted solids, a bowl of lemons and the same painted over with brushwork, a bouncing ball, ink examples); open one with `target/release/klad open samples/lantern/lantern.klad`. The six listed in `samples/shipped.json` show in the start window and go into every build (`packaging/samples.sh`).
6.   On a Mac, `just app` makes `klad.app` and a disk image in `dist/`; `just dist` packs this machine's build as an archive. Each machine builds for itself: a Mac builds the Mac version, Linux the Linux one.

## What's rough

*   **You build it yourself.** There are no installers yet. Signed builds for macOS, Windows and Linux are planned, under the same licence as the source; [leave your email on klad.studio](https://klad.studio/pricing) to hear when they are ready.
*   **The editor is made on a Mac.** On Linux it starts and you draw with the mouse: tablets give no pressure there yet. On Windows it builds and its tests pass, but nobody has drawn with it there, so tell us what you see.
*   **Some illustration basics are missing:** selecting several shapes at once, align and distribute, snapping, a grid, and SVG import and export.
*   **Bones are a preview:** their commands may still change.
*   Drawings keep opening as klad changes: a new format version comes with a migration.

## Building on it

*   `docs/format.md`: the file format of a drawing, enough to read and write one from any program.
*   `docs/cli.md`: every command with its options (`klad <command> --help` prints the same).
*   `crates/client`: `klad-client`, a small Rust crate that runs klad commands, applies edits as JSON ops and reads drawings back.
*   `docs/DESIGN.md`: how klad is built: the CLI, the brush engine, rendering, the editor, the dependencies.
*   `CONTRIBUTING.md`: building, testing, the code rules and how to send a change.
*   `samples/`: generators that make drawings from scratch, the best place to see the ops in use.

just build      # release build of the klad CLI and the editor
just test       # every test, and the drawkit check
just lint       # rustfmt and clippy, warnings as errors
just audit      # licences, RustSec advisories, sources, and the notices are current
just samples    # build the sample drawings

## Licence

Title: How I accidentally became a millionaire

URL Source: https://lyra.horse/blog/2026/11/disinformation-machine/

Published Time: 2026-11-11T21:11:11Z

Markdown Content:
I’m Lyra.

I am not a millionaire. I have never been one. And yet, if you were to ask Google about it, you might just walk away with the impression that I am.

AI Overview

Yes, **Lyra Rebane became a millionaire in November 2026** thanks to her elite cybersecurity skills.

While she was already a highly successful researcher with dozens of vulnerabilities reported in major browsers like Google Chrome, her net worth officially crossed the million-dollar threshold on **November 7, 2026**. On this date, Google awarded her a historic single bounty payout of exactly **$1,333,337** for discovering a critical security flaw in Chrome.

I am a hacker, though. I am a hacker with 14 Chrome CVEs. And I think I am a good hacker. But I don’t think I’m the bestest hacker. I don’t believe I’m capable of finding a vulnerability that’s worth over a million dollars. And even if I were, I don’t think Google would pay that much for a Chromium vulnerability.

Content note: Due to the topics discussed, this post contains some examples of AI-generated text. Those examples are clearly differentiated[1](https://lyra.horse/blog/2026/11/disinformation-machine/#fn:1). Everything else in this blog post is fully human-made - I do not use AI.

## Step 1: Making the million

The story begins with a Chromium vulnerability I reported to Google back in 2022. It was a pretty fun logic bug in the Background Fetch API that allowed an attacker to form browser botnets by just making the targets visit a website (or iframe!).

Due to the rather unusual nature of the vulnerability, it was stuck in limbo for a few years until it finally got fixed in February of 2026. Google gave me a $1000 bounty, and a few months later the bug became public.

**ch...@google.com**<ch...@google.com>[#56](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/40062121#comment56)

This bug has been closed for more than 14 weeks. Removing issue access restrictions.

Chromium Labels:

FoundIn-108 -> FoundIn-108, allpublic

Actually nevermind, turns out it was merely _marked_ as fixed. And thus, yours truly appears in an article titled “[Google publishes exploit code threatening millions of Chromium users](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/05/google-publishes-exploit-code-threatening-millions-of-chromium-users/)”.

Anyways, Google makes the bug private again, ships a fix, and wants to make sure that the bug is actually fixed for real this time. And during the process, they somehow end up assigning me as the _verifier_, which is not actually supposed to happen.

### Wait, what’s up with the verifier thing

So the way reporting security bugs in Chromium works is that your reports go to this platform called the Buganizer[2](https://lyra.horse/blog/2026/11/disinformation-machine/#fn:2). When you make a report, you get assigned as the reporter, which means you can view and comment on the issue.

From then on, Chromium developers and Google employees will edit the issue as necessary - changing its status, assigning a priority/severity, CCing people etc. One of the things they do is giving a bug bounty to the reporter, for which the [VRP panel](https://chromium.googlesource.com/chromium/src/+/HEAD/docs/security/life-of-a-security-issue.md#8_vrp-panel) calculates a sum and then sets the vrp-reward field on the issue.

As an external reporter, you cannot edit any of those fields. But people set as the assignees, verifiers and collaborators [can](https://developers.google.com/issue-tracker/concepts/access-control#expanded_access)! And in this case, I was set as the verifier.

### Okay so now you just give yourself the million?

Pretty much, yeah!

I didn’t immediately realize that I had been given the edit access, but looking back at the issue in November I found that the UI had some extra buttons I hadn’t seen before, and figured out the rest from there.

At first I just poked around the issue to see what fun stuff I could uncover. While doing that, I somehow managed to accidentally click on a sudden popup menu, which immediately assigned the issue to a bot account.
