Title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG

URL Source: https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval

Markdown Content:
Maximum inner product search (MIPS) sits at the core of recommendation systems, search, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Given a query vector, MIPS systems search within a database of millions of candidate key vectors for the one that best matches the query. The original data point associated with that best-matching key is then used to handle the query: in RAG, the document that is best suited to answer the question is typically prefixed to the query.

As the number of keys grows to millions and vector dimensions reach thousands, the computational cost of running an exhaustive comparison of the query to all keys grows dramatically. Numerous approximate methods have been proposed to trade off accuracy for speed using clustering and quantization. While these baseline methods focus on the properties of the set of keys to build up clever indexing structures, their geometric arguments loosely assume that the set of queries itself will resemble that found in keys, or bypass any considerations about what the queries will look like. This can be problematic on two fronts: In the crucial RAG case, queries arise from short user-generated questions, whereas keys represent long, informative, and curated pieces of text, making keys and queries substantially different. Additionally, most MIPS use cases deployed in production target an existing base of users with a stable, well-characterized query distribution — a signal that generic, query-agnostic methods leave untapped. Crafting methods that work best for a likely source of inputs — rather than aiming for good performance on all possible inputs — is a central tenet of modern machine learning that helps redirect compute resources more efficiently.

In [Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/amortizing-inner-product-search), a paper presented at ICML 2026, researchers from Apple train small neural networks (NNs) — once, offline, for a fixed database of keys — that learn how to route queries toward their best match faster. Their approach trades off an upfront amortization cost to understand how typical queries tend to be matched in exchange for faster, more accurate retrieval at inference time through these small NNs.

A fundamental principle in MIPS is to leverage the geometry of the set of keys to speed up search: Typical MIPS systems split the set of keys into _k_ clusters — _k_ is typically much smaller than the total number of keys _n_ — keeping track of a representative centroid for each cluster. When receiving a new query, the system compares it with these _k_ centroids. The query is then routed toward the cluster of the representative centroid it is closest to, and subsequently compared exhaustively with all keys stored in that cluster. If the database has _n_ keys and _k_ evenly distributed clusters, the effective number of keys that will be considered in that second step is on the order of _n_/_k_ — a factor-of- _k_ speedup when compared to the _n_ comparisons done in the naive exhaustive approach. Unfortunately, this routing mechanism can result in errors, since centroid routing is not an exact approach, as illustrated in [Figure 1](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval#figure1) below.

Figure 1: Geometric approaches to search can fail and miss nearest neighbors. This is due to their reliance on partitioning the space based on distances to centroids. In the animation, a nearest neighbor is missed as it is not associated with the nearest centroid.

What makes MIPS interesting from a machine learning perspective is that it is built on a mathematical structure that had been largely overlooked before this work: The function that maps a query to the largest inner product with any key in a set is the [support function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Support_function) of that set, a well-studied object in convex analysis. This function has two important properties: First, it is convex, so it can be approximated by a class of neural networks specifically designed for convex functions, [input convex neural networks (ICNNs)](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v70/amos17b.html). Second, the gradient of that support function at any query returns the best-matching key itself.

The broad idea behind this work is to _learn_ a neural network that can mimic the ground-truth support function (or its gradient directly) for a much lower computational cost. This can be achieved through a classical ML technique known as regression: one simply needs to precompute a large number of training examples formed by sampling input vectors (user queries) and pair them with the relevant output signal produced by MIPS (either the optimal score or the optimal key vector itself). All that is then needed is to train a suitably parameterized neural network to replicate the output given the input.

If the regression problem were to be solved perfectly, according to the mathematical approach outlined above, the same neural network that is trained to mimic the support function could also output the optimal key by evaluating its gradient (through automatic differentiation). In practice, we observe that training separate, specialized networks for each of these two tasks works best:

The **SupportNet** neural network architecture can learn the support function directly, using a (loosely constrained) ICNN. The approach is mathematically principled and aligns with the convex structure of the problem. We find that this approach can shine when used to compute one support function per data cluster to improve routing quality.

**KeyNet** models learn to _directly_ output the best-matching key vector when fed a query. A consistency loss derived from Euler’s theorem for homogeneous functions keeps their predictions geometrically grounded in the underlying support function, even though no convexity is explicitly enforced.

Both models are trained on examples drawn from the relevant query distribution: for each sampled query, the ground-truth best match is computed once via exhaustive search and stored, creating a supervised dataset that captures the MIPS solution landscape for the distribution of queries that actually matter.

As shown in [Figure 1](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval#figure1), the simplest way to handle larger scales is to split the keys into clusters, compare the query to each cluster’s centroid, and route the query to the most promising clusters based on these _k_ scores. This provides a cheap yet coarse rule that can be prone to mistakes because a centroid alone cannot account for the spread of its cluster. Indeed, a cluster can hold a key that sits far from its own centroid yet close to the query, and when the query is near such an outlier, centroid routing scores the cluster low and skips it, missing the true best match.

If one were given access to the support function of each cluster, then one would instead be able to do exact routing, since each support function quantifies exactly to what extent any key within each cluster can match the query with a large score. This is illustrated in [Figure 2](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval#figure2), in which the support function of each of the four clusters is plotted for a query that varies in the space of embeddings.

Figure 2: Relying on distances to centroids can be misleading as those distances do not account for every key in each cluster. Given access to each cluster’s support function, assignment can be made based on how well a given query matches any key in a cluster.

Leaning on this theoretical insight, we propose to learn these _k_ support functions jointly with a trained SupportNet that can output _k_ scores at once. We can then use the largest of these _k_ scores to route any new query instead. The SupportNet model can answer a more useful question than a simple comparison to the centroid can: “How good is the _best_ key inside this cluster for this query?” SupportNets are trained in a classic machine learning fashion, also known as regression: we generate sample queries that are drawn from the distribution (typically embeddings for text queries), compute the ground-truth support functions at those queries, and train a neural network to replicate these values.

Figure 3: SupportNets approximate the support functions of each cluster and assign queries to clusters based on the best match with any key, not only centroids as typical geometric approaches do.

We trained SupportNets of increasing sizes (XS, S, M, and L → 1%, 5%, 10%, and 20% of the database size) on [Natural Questions](https://huggingface.co/datasets/BeIR/nq-generated-queries) partitioned into 128 clusters. Natural Questions is a retrieval benchmark that pairs general-knowledge questions with passages from a large document database, roughly 2.6M unique passages in our setup.

[Figure 4](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval#figure4) below shows the retrieval performance in terms of recall as a function of different notions of cost. Routing recall is the fraction of queries whose true partition, the one holding the exact best key, lands among those the router chooses to probe. For both plots, an exhaustive search is carried out in the top-_s_ clusters matched with the query, where _s_ grows as powers of two _(1, 2, 4, 8, …, 128)_. Naturally, all methods reach a recall of 1 when they survey all 128 clusters.

The first tab shows that for a fixed retrieval performance the learned routers reach it at lower latency than centroid routing. The small SupportNet model hits 95% routing recall about 1.9× faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms), and gains are even greater with the large model, which hits 97% in 1.74 ms. This plot explicitly factors in the additional compute incurred by running our small NNs rather than simply comparing to centroids.

The plot on the second tab looks exclusively at routing quality, neglecting the overhead incurred by running NNs. At a fixed budget of explored clusters, they find the right partition more often: scanning just 5% of the database, the learned routers recover the true partition ~90–93% of the time — up to 92.6% for the mid-size (M) — versus 87.5% for the centroid baseline.

Figure 4: Routing performance (recall) due to SupportNets of various sizes versus latency or the fraction of the database we allow the router to scan. Routers, all with a depth of 16 layers, are trained on a 128-cluster Natural Questions dataset. SupportNets dominate the centroid router: given a latency target, one can get a higher recall with a SupportNet or conversely, that recall can be achieved at lower latency by a SupportNet than by a centroid router.

SupportNet routing replaces the simple centroid-based routing found in existing inverted file index (IVF) systems. With KeyNet, we can also keep the IVF system as is and just feed it a modified version of the query. In that scenario, KeyNet works naturally as a _“query rewriter”_ in front of a standard approximate search index: predict where the best match is likely to be in embedding space, then ask your favorite IVF system to look there instead of starting from the original query. Because the IVF index is highly optimized, it can find the result faster when assisted by KeyNet. We also rely on regression to train KeyNets, as summarized in [Figure 5](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/faster-retrieval#figure5): sample queries are matched with their ground-truth, best-matching key, and the KeyNet neural network is trained to reproduce that association.

Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
Nvidia is reportedly planning to oust its co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang, who has led the company for the last 33 years,
the Wall Street Journal reports
. Sources told the newspaper that the Nvidia board is meeting as soon as Wednesday to determine Huang’s future at the company.
On Sunday, Huang admitted to having an extramarital affair with a woman purported by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. On Wednesday evening, the New York Times
reported
that Huang also had an affair with an executive who reports to him.
Nvidia has become one of the most valuable companies in the world as it designs the chips that power the AI boom, but in the midst of Huang’s
ongoing scandal
, Nvidia stock fell
about 8%
in after hours trading on Wednesday. The stock is down about 11% in the past five days.
Huang famously delegates very little and has about 60 direct reports, he
has said
. The company also has not had an obvious successor or a succession plan. According to Bloomberg, Nvidia is working with an outside firm to identify candidates that could
potentially replace
Huang as CEO.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
It’s that time of year again: Thousands of delegates, lobbyists, and journalists are gathered for the annual UN climate talks, taking place this time in Antalya, Turkey.
COP31 officially kicked off on November 8, marking the beginning of negotiations on one of the biggest stages of the climate world. Turkey and Australia are cohosting this year’s talks, which are scheduled to wrap up on November 20.
This annual gathering can often serve as an indicator of where the world stands on addressing and adapting to the climate crisis. And this year’s talks are sure to be a doozy—expect a lot of back and forth on fossil fuels and climate finance in particular. Here’s what you should know about COP31.
In recent years, the tension always feels high when COP rolls around. (COP stands for “Conference of the Parties.”) But this year feels especially charged: The world is still grappling with the ongoing war in Iran, which has disrupted the Middle East and sent economic shock waves around the world as energy prices have spiked.
This year’s COP will be the second without a formal delegation from the US. President Trump formally withdrew the country from the Paris Agreement earlier this year and is in the process of withdrawing from the UN Framework Committee on Climate Change. That’s the treaty that allows formal participation in negotiations.
Meanwhile, things aren’t looking good for the Paris Agreement, which was established at UN climate talks 11 years ago, setting a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 °C over preindustrial levels. In a report published in September, the UN Environment Program acknowledged that global warming is set to exceed that 1.5 °C goal, “likely within the next few years.”
So as climate talks kick off, there’s an obvious, urgent question looming about how to quickly cut emissions to limit warming. There’s also the major issue of how to pay for efforts to address emissions and to help a warming world endure the inevitable damage.
Two years ago, talks ended in a goal of mobilizing $300 billion per year by 2035 to help pay to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change. (Rich nations provided $136.7 billion in 2024,
according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.
) And last year, the COP30 agreement included a goal of tripling the money for adaptation over that period. (Such funding has been
quite flat
over the past few years.)
The world got a tragic reminder of just how high the stakes are earlier this year, when
a glacier collapse
caused devastating flooding in the Himalayas. The flood killed approximately 1,500 people, left over 5,000 missing, and caused nearly $5 billion in damage. The UN loss and damages fund committed $20 million to
helping Nepal
recover (less than 1% of the total estimated cost to the country).
Another key trend to watch is how the formal negotiations engage with the topic of fossil fuels. Three years ago, the final agreement text explicitly called for a transition away from them. But it felt as if things took a step back last year, when the final agreement didn’t even mention the phrase “fossil fuels” once. This will be an interesting conversation, especially because cohosts Turkey and Australia have both faced criticism over their relationships with these fuels—Australia is a major exporter of coal and natural gas, and Turkey’s grid relies heavily on fossil fuels, including coal.
Outside the formal negotiations, COP31 president Murat Kurum, Turkey’s environment minister, is spearheading a side agenda, including two informal initiatives that will be worth watching. These wouldn’t be part of the official agreement text, but countries could sign on to signal support.
One is a pledge to make AI more sustainable; this is almost comically squishy, even as voluntary COP pledges go. The text includes explicit wording that it creates no new obligations for countries, so don’t expect anything resembling enforcement there.
The COP leadership is also pushing to make electricity a larger part of member countries’ energy use. Today, only about 23% of global energy is used in the form of electricity. Fossil fuels, like gasoline in vehicles or natural gas for heating, make up the bulk of the rest. Shifting to more electricity use, and relying on cleaner sources for that electricity, could help drive down emissions. The new pledge’s target is for electricity to make up 35% of total energy consumption by 2035.
With leadership billing this as an “implementation COP,” it would be great to see some real, tangible progress on the global challenge of addressing climate change. I’m not expecting anything groundbreaking, but we’ll be tuned in to see what the final agreement shapes up to be.
